abstract: • UAV-mounted system enables autonomous in situ soil phosphorus sensing. • Electrochemical probing overcomes limitations of imaging-based nutrient estimation. • Spatially informed machine learning converts sparse samples into coherent P maps. • Field validation across Canada and Tanzania achieved F1-scores up to 0.91. • Framework supports scalable, data-driven fertilizer management systems. Accurate spatial mapping of soil phosphorus remains challenging due to the high cost and limited spatial density of laboratory soil analyses and the poor performance of remote-sensing approaches for phosphorus estimation. This study presents a UAV-mounted soil sensing system that integrates autonomous mechanical probing with in-situ electrochemical measurement and spatial machine learning to enable high-resolution phosphorus mapping under field conditions. The platform combines a lightweight drone-deployable probing mechanism, an ion-selective electrochemical probe, onboard control electronics, and wireless telemetry to collect GPS-referenced soil nutrient measurements during automated flight operations. Field experiments were conducted at two contrasting agricultural sites: a vineyard in British Columbia, Canada, and an intensively managed flower farm in Arusha, Tanzania. Three complementary datasets were generated to evaluate spatial nutrient structure at both location and within-location scales. Spatial feature engineering incorporated positional geometry and neighborhood statistics, and spatial autocorrelation was assessed using Moran’s I and variogram analysis. Random Forest classifiers were trained using spatially grouped cross-validation to prevent performance inflation due to spatial dependence. Across study sites, the proposed approach achieved weighted F1-scores ranging from 0.82 to 0.91, representing improvements of 25–40% over baseline classifiers. The resulting phosphorus maps were spatially coherent and agronomically plausible, successfully identifying low-phosphorus zones in the Canadian vineyard despite limited nutrient variability, and distinct low- and high-phosphorus regions in the Tanzanian field where fertility gradients were stronger. Analysis of feature importance highlighted the dominant role of local spatial contrast and neighborhood information, underscoring the importance of explicitly modeling spatial context when using in situ electrochemical sensors. The results demonstrate that coupling UAV-based automated soil probing with spatially informed machine learning provides an effective pathway for transforming sparse physical measurements into continuous phosphorus distribution maps. This integrated sensing-to-mapping framework offers a scalable foundation for site-specific nutrient management and can be extended to additional soil properties and precision agriculture applications.

title: RapeseedNet: a lightweight deep learning model for rapeseed quality detection based on near-infrared spectroscopy
abstract: Rapid detection of key quality indicators of rapeseed and edge deployment are crucial for improving oil processing efficiency, ensuring feed safety, and optimizing storage management. This study analyzed the responses of oil content, protein content, glucosinolate content, and moisture content of 681 rapeseed samples from multiple varieties and regions to near-infrared spectroscopy (NIR). It also explored the effects of different preprocessing methods and data partitioning strategies on model performance. To address the limitations of traditional detection methods (time-consuming, destructive) and insufficient generalization of existing models, a base model RapeseedNet-Base was constructed by fusing ResNet modules, Transformer encoder layers, and Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP). This model outperformed traditional machine learning methods in quality prediction tasks, with determination coefficients (R2) of 0.893, 0.818, 0.917, and 0.815 for oil content, protein content, glucosinolate content, and moisture content prediction on the test set, respectively. Through multi-scale knowledge distillation and unstructured pruning optimization, it was upgraded to a lightweight model RapeseedNet, with a 61.2% reduction in parameters, 56% shorter computation time, and no significant loss of accuracy. After deploying the model to a portable detector, on-site verification showed R2 = 0.867 for oil content prediction and R2 = 0.819 for glucosinolate content prediction, with a single detection time of approximately 15 s, meeting real-time detection needs. This study provides strong technical support for rapid rapeseed quality detection and precise processing, and also offers a reference for non-destructive detection of other oilseed crops.

title: Key-waypoint-guided global coverage path planning system for unmanned ground vehicles in orchards
abstract: Global path planning is crucial for the autonomous navigation of orchard vehicles. Yet, how to leverage global structural information to manage task sequencing and generate coverage paths across the entire operation area remains underexplored. This study proposes a DBSCAN–OBB–based method to extract tree-row endpoints and automatically generate key waypoints constrained by vehicle parameters. The coverage operation is formulated as a kinematically constrained shortest-path problem, and the optimal waypoint sequence is obtained using the CGB algorithm. A global path planner, MultiPointPlanner, constructs and concatenates inter-row and headland segments, yielding smooth and feasible global paths. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieved a mean waypoint error of ≤ 0.19 m. For orchards of different scales, the CGB algorithm generated optimal waypoint traversal sequences, achieving up to 39.7% non-productive travel reduction compared to the row-by-row rule, while ensuring equivalent optimality within a computation time of ≤ 0.1 s. In path-tracking experiments, the planned global paths exhibit low curvature fluctuation and consistent heading. In headland regions, the proposed planner keeps trajectories away from high-risk boundaries, allowing the vehicle to follow smoothly under continuous curvature constraints. The row-switching time is reduced by 61.1%, and the minimum obstacle clearance is increased by 64.0%. Across the entire operation area, the number of reversals and manual takeovers was substantially reduced, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed approach in achieving geometrically smooth, kinematically feasible, and risk-avoiding coverage paths.

title: Vibration transmission characteristics of Camellia oleifera tree under excitation
abstract: Clarifying the impact of excitation and tree structural parameters on the vibration transmission characteristics of trees is crucial for enhancing the efficiency of vibration harvesting. In this study, the mass distributions of the fruits, buds, and leaves on the canopy branches were used to construct a vibration model, and the low-order natural frequency range of the branches was determined to be 1.39 ∼ 11.58 Hz. Vibration transmission tests revealed that frequency, amplitude, excitation distance, and crown diameter positively influence crown acceleration, while tree height and trunk diameter have a negative influence. Vibration frequency, tree height, crown diameter, and trunk diameter positively influence the energy decay rate, whereas vibration amplitude and excitation distance have a negative influence. Canopy acceleration and energy decay rate are most strongly affected by frequency, amplitude and excitation distance. With a vibration frequency of 8.96 Hz, an amplitude of 50 mm, and an excitation distance of 60 cm, the canopy acceleration was maximized at 67.12 m/s2, while minimum energy decay rate was 68.43%. The optimum operating parameters of the harvesting device were reached at a frequency of 8.7 ∼ 9.6 Hz, an amplitude of 47 ∼ 50 mm, and an excitation distance of 53 ∼ 60 cm. These research findings provide an important reference for the development and field application of Camellia oleifera vibration harvesting devices.

title: Breakage mitigation optimization strategy for a spiral-groove wheel fertilizer distributor based on a controlled-release fertilizer breakage model
abstract: Controlled-release fertilizers play a crucial role in developing efficient and sustainable agriculture. However, during mechanized application, controlled-release fertilizers are prone to breakage under complex multi-source mechanical forces, which compromises their release performance. To address this issue, an equivalent breakage model for controlled-release fertilizers was developed, and a breakage-reduction optimization strategy was proposed for a helical-groove metering wheel fertilizer applicator. First, the physical and geometric properties of particles were determined through laboratory measurements, and a corresponding simulation particle model was established. Second, key parameters of the equivalent breakage model were obtained from uniaxial compression and drop-weight impact tests, enabling accurate reproduction of the particle breakage behavior. Third, single-factor and multi-factor optimization simulations were performed using the discrete element method. The metering wheel rotational speed, helical angle, and fertilizer outlet tongue inclination were selected as test factors, while the discharge rate and proportion broken were used as evaluation indices. Furthermore, response surface methodology was applied to identify the optimal breakage-reduction strategy: a metering wheel rotational speed of 43 r/min, a helical angle of 70°, and a fertilizer outlet tongue inclination of 22°. Finally, bench tests were conducted to validate the accuracy of both the simulation model and the optimal parameter combination, yielding mean relative errors of 5.02% for discharge rate and 5.54% for proportion broken. The findings provide theoretical support and technical guidance for improving breakage reduction and application efficiency, as well as for optimizing the design of fertilizer applicators for controlled-release fertilizers.

title: A machine learning-based wearable system for automated detection of sheep parturition events using accelerometer data
abstract: • Wearable accelerometer technology enables the detection of lambing events by monitoring ewe discomfort and lying bouts. • A learning model was developed to define time intervals leading up to lambing. • The learning model identifies time intervals based on lying bout patterns. • The detection system provides near real-time lambing detection. The quality and safety of sheep farming increasingly depend on automated monitoring systems, with parturition detection representing a critical challenge due to its direct impact on lamb survival. This study presents the development and evaluation of two machine learning approaches for predicting sheep parturition: a lightweight model designed for deployment on collar-mounted devices with limited computational resources, and a full-featured model intended for scenarios without such constraints. The models were developed using data from 53 parturition events collected via collar-mounted accelerometers and thermometers, within a system that supports real-time data acquisition, processing, and visualization of parturition predictions. The lightweight model, operating under strict computational and memory limitations, achieved an accuracy of 0.74 and a Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.71. In contrast, the full-featured model delivered superior performance, reaching an accuracy of 0.81 and an MCC of 0.79 when predicting time to birth up to 11 h in advance. Additionally, temporal filtering optimization contributed to stable performance in extended validation scenarios for both models. The work included the development of a detection tool based on the use of an MQTT broker, that includes two subscribers that perform detection, and alarm triggering, and a producer that streams monitoring data gathered by the the collars. Overall, this work advances precision livestock farming by offering two practical solutions for automated parturition monitoring, enabling farmers to select either a resource-efficient or a high-performance approach according to their specific operational requirements and available infrastructure.

title: Beetroot type classification based on 3D structure constructed with neural radiance fields
abstract: The phenotypic traits of beetroot are of great significance for revealing the relationship between their morphology and functional traits, as well as for the breeding high-quality cultivars. The 3D models can provide a more comprehensive and accurate description of beetroot structural features, offering richer phenotypic information compared to traditional 2D imaging methods. This study developed a novel framework that integrates Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) for high-fidelity 3D reconstruction, multi-dimensional phenotypic traits extraction and an end to end network, named as Point-SugarRoot based on point cloud and deep learning for precise classification. The results indicated that NeRF-derived phenotypic traits strongly correlated with actual measurements, achieving R2 values exceeding 0.92. NeRF-reconstructed point clouds exhibited less noise, with an average C2C distance of 0.11 cm, a SC rate of 94.6%, and a 12.9% reduction in reconstruction time, outperforming the Structure from Motion (SfM)-Multi-View Stereo (MVS) method in precision and efficiency. The Point-SugarRoot network surpassed the baseline PointNet++ model, delivering Precision, Recall, F1 score, and Balanced Accuracy of 91.3%, 90.8%, 91.1%, and 93.0%, respectively, and outperformed phenotype- and 2D image-based classification methods by 13% to 33% across all metrics. This research presents a novel solution for high-fidelity 3D reconstruction and phenotypic analysis of beetroots, while also providing valuable technical insights for cultivar breeding and crop management.

title: Plant 3D-2D-ResNet-SE: Monitoring the changes of leaf water content and chlorophyll in Betula luminifera seedlings during drought stress
abstract: Betula luminifera, a tree species of notable ecological and economic value, has leaf water content (LWC) and leaf chlorophyll content (LCC) as vital phenotypic traits, crucial for plant health assessment and forestry productivity. This study proposed a hybrid convolutional neural network (CNN)-based model utilizing hyperspectral images as inputs to directly predict the LWC and LCC of Betula luminifera leaves. The model accepts hyperspectral images as input without the tedious steps of manually selecting regions of interest (ROI) and converting hyperspectral data into average spectra in traditional methods, and directly predicts the LWC and LCC of Betula luminifera leaves. The hybrid convolutional neural network model combines 3D convolution kernels to capture spectral information and 2D convolution kernels to extract spatial features, effectively improving the accuracy of prediction. To refine feature selection further, this study uniquely incorporated Competitive Adaptive Reweighted Sampling (CARS) and the Successive Projection Algorithm (SPA) band-selection methods. Shapley values were used to assess the relevance of each wavelength, identifying those most critical to prediction. Five-fold cross-validation was incorporated into the results to reduce the randomness of data splitting. Results show that the 3D-2D-ResNet-SE model demonstrates outstanding performance in predicting LWC and LCC, with R2 reaching 0.86 and 0.85, respectively, marking the first instance of regression predictions from direct hyperspectral image inputs. The study confirms the efficacy of SPA and CARS in selecting key hyperspectral image bands and introduces a novel hybrid deep learning framework for accurate physiological parameter detection in Betula luminifera leaves. This method provides substantive advancements for plant health monitoring and seedling management, with significant potential to support the development of precision agriculture.

title: TARAG: A time-aware retrieval-augmented generation framework for supporting precision crop pest and disease management through large language models
abstract: Plant diseases and pests cause significant annual crop losses, severely threatening global food security. To mitigate crop losses, large language models (LLMs) demonstrate the ability to alleviate challenges in accessing precise farming support by acting as intelligent assistants that provide farmers with timely and precise decision support services. However, existing efforts still fall short in precision due to the neglect of time-sensitive nature in agricultural practices. They implicitly treat domain knowledge as time-irrelevant, ignoring the impact of crop phenology and pest life stages in their generated recommendations. To address this challenge, we propose a Time-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework (TARAG), comprising a time-aware knowledge base construction module, a hybrid retrieval module, and a time-based generation module to provide precise pest management suggestions. Firstly, the time-aware knowledge base construction module constructs a time-annotated knowledge base from unstructured documents to provide supplementary agricultural knowledge. Secondly, the hybrid retrieval module performs coarse-grained sparse retrieval to ensure relevance, with a time-sensitive re-ranking stage that refines the results to achieve both semantic relevance retrieval and time alignment with user queries. Finally, the time-aware generation module leverages the top-k retrieved documents and an instruction prompt to produce the final suggestion. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we contribute TAQA, the first bilingual, time-annotated agricultural question-answering dataset. Experiments demonstrate that TARAG significantly outperforms state-of-the-art RAG frameworks in retrieval precision and suggestion quality, with 99.14% retrieval recall and an F1 score of 66.85% for generated suggestions. The implementation and datasets for this work are available in https://github.com/lee-hash1/agri_rag.

title: Research on a cloud-edge collaborative system for long-term behavior analysis in intensive pig farms under multi-resource constraints
abstract: In intensive gestation-crate pig houses, long-term behavior analysis is jointly constrained by edge-side compute (CPU-only), uplink bandwidth, edge storage, and cloud GPU throughput, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve continuous capture, stable uploading, and timely inference. This paper proposes a constraint-aware edge-cloud collaborative framework targeting end-to-end sustainable throughput and long-term reliable operation: on the source/edge side, acquisition settings aligned with the model input (224 × 224 pixels, 4 fps) and a two-stage ROI cropping pipeline are employed to reduce redundant inputs; on the cloud side, window-level inference is employed with event-level temporal fusion, converting computational load into controllable window throughput; on the transmission side, a queue-based cache management mechanism with bandwidth-aware uploading (with threshold-based eviction) is introduced, keeping the cache bounded and enabling backlog drainage during network outage, congestion, and recovery. Deployment and experimental evaluation in a pig house show that, compared to the baseline, the proposed source-side reduction and two-stage ROI design reduce CPU overhead per stream to about one-third, data generation to about 1/11.6, and average transmission bitrate to about 1/39.7; meanwhile, on the transmission side, queue-based caching and bandwidth-aware uploading ensure stable uploading under network fluctuations and improve system robustness; cloud window throughput increases from about 20 to about 180, yielding an approximately 9 × improvement in processing capacity.

title: Leaf area extraction framework: Transformer-based segmentation and geometric-based completion approaches for accurate extraction of field maize leaf area from point clouds
abstract: The accurate determination of the maize leaf area is crucial for precision agriculture and yield optimization. Three-dimensional point-cloud technology provides a non-destructive and efficient alternative to traditional methods, which are often inefficient and inaccurate. This study aims to develop a robust field-compatible framework for maize leaf area extraction. It focuses on two key challenges: interference from environmental factors, such as strong sunlight, during point-cloud collection, and the mutual occlusion of leaves under complex field conditions. To address the first challenge, we propose a structured light-based point-cloud acquisition system that is optimized to minimize sunlight interference, thus enabling high-fidelity data collection in outdoor environments. We then utilize a Transformer-enhanced semantic segmentation network to isolate individual leaves accurately, achieving high precision across key evaluation metrics, including the precision, recall, F1-score, and intersection over union. The leaf area is subsequently calculated through triangulation. Our analysis revealed distinct performance variations between the vegetative and reproductive growth phases. While the framework demonstrated exceptional accuracy during the early stages, the performance declined significantly during the tasselling-to-maturity phase, owing to increased leaf occlusion and geometric complexity. To address this issue, we introduce two novel geometric processing algorithms: leaf contour completion and leaf body completion. These algorithms collectively enhance the accuracy, and the improvement effect becomes more significant as the point-cloud loss intensifies. Consequently, the most pronounced improvements are observed in the later growth stages. This work contributes to precision agriculture by establishing a growth-stage-adaptive leaf area extraction framework that aligns technical innovations with agronomic needs.

title: Design and implementation of an orchard variable spray system based on visual recognition and fuzzy adaptive decoupling
abstract: To improve the precision of spray operations and pesticide utilization efficiency in citrus orchards, this study developed a variable-rate spraying system integrating canopy perception, disease recognition, and fuzzy self-tuning PID decoupling control. The system adopts a dual-mode spraying strategy: during critical phenological stages, whole-orchard preventive spraying is implemented according to canopy characteristics, whereas during non-preventive periods, localized precision target spraying is performed based on real-time disease recognition results. An improved YOLOv8n-DE model was evaluated using a self-built dataset containing 6050 citrus disease images, and the overall system performance was validated through simulations, indoor calibration experiments, and field trials. The results showed that the YOLOv8n-DE model achieved a mean average precision of 97.3% on the test set. The proposed control algorithm reduced the settling times for flow rate and pressure regulation to 50.0 ms and 33.25 ms, respectively. Indoor experiments determined that the appropriate operating parameters for field application were a spraying distance of 1.0 m and a travelling speed of 0.5 m s−1. Field experiments showed that the canopy-based spraying mode achieved a droplet deposition density of 30.98 droplets cm−2 and a coverage rate of 54.67%, while the disease-based spraying mode achieved a droplet deposition density of 40.27 droplets cm−2 and a coverage rate of 43.01%. Under disease-recognition-based spraying conditions, the droplet deposition utilization efficiency and pesticide-saving rate of the system reached 66.53% and 71.27%, respectively. This system can provide technical support for intelligent pesticide application in citrus orchards by integrating preventive protection with precise intervention.

title: Non-contact technologies for cattle monitoring: advances and challenges towards precision livestock farming
abstract: Precision livestock farming has become essential for sustainable production, animal welfare, and management efficiency. Non-contact monitoring technologies have emerged as promising solutions. Compared with wearable or invasive devices, non-contact approaches enable continuous and stable monitoring without disturbing natural behaviors, thereby minimizing stress and welfare risks. This review provides a comprehensive review of research progress on non-contact technologies in cattle farming, covering five core domains: individual identification, morphological trait assessment, behavioral analysis, vital signs monitoring, and disease detection. Furthermore, key bottlenecks hindering large-scale deployment are identified, and future development prospects are outlined across four dimensions: data resources, algorithmic performance, evaluation frameworks, and system integration. This review aims to foster interdisciplinary collaboration and technical advancement of non-contact technologies in precision cattle farming through systematic synthesis and critical discussion, offering valuable insights for both practical applications and future research.

title: An adaptive experience-based discrete genetic algorithm for multi-trip picking robot task scheduling in smart orchards
abstract: The continuous innovation of smart robotic technologies is driving the development of smart orchards, significantly enhancing the potential for automated harvesting systems. While multi-robot systems offer promising solutions to address labor shortages and rising costs, the efficient scheduling of these systems presents complex optimization challenges. This research investigates the multi-trip picking robot task scheduling (MTPRTS) problem. The problem is characterized by its provision for robot redeployment while maintaining strict adherence to makespan constraints, and encompasses the interdependencies among robot weight, robot load, and energy consumption, thus introducing substantial computational challenges that demand sophisticated optimization algorithms.To effectively tackle this complexity, metaheuristic approaches, which often utilize local search mechanisms, are widely employed. Despite the critical role of local search in vehicle routing problems, most existing algorithms are hampered by redundant local operations, leading to slower search processes and higher risks of local optima, particularly in large-scale scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we propose an adaptive experience-based discrete genetic algorithm (AEDGA) that introduces three key innovations: (1) integrated load-distance balancing initialization method, (2) a clustering-based local search mechanism, and (3) an experience-based adaptive selection strategy. To ensure solution feasibility under makespan constraints, we develop a solution repair strategy implemented through three distinct frameworks. Comprehensive experiments on 18 proposed test instances and 24 existing test problems demonstrate that AEDGA significantly outperforms eight state-of-the-art algorithms.

title: Fish body midline segmentation using binary search
abstract: Body and caudal fin locomotion is ubiquitous in aquatic vertebrates, and kinematic models describing it are used in robotics, biomechanics and fisheries research. This paper presents a new algorithm to translate continuous body midlines of fish into a series of interconnected segments by identifying favorable joint positions along the body. The algorithm employs binary search to generate parsimonious kinematic models, aiming at minimizing the number of segments yet keeping approximation error below a user-defined threshold. To achieve this, the algorithm maximizes the length of each segment by determining the most distal joint position through repetitive shrinking of the search space. Theoretical and empirical analysis using two different datasets show that the binary search algorithm is substantially faster when compared to segment growing algorithm, which employs linear search to generate its models. There is four-fold improvement in computation time when generating models with less than 10 segments, which are typically sufficient to describe fish and fish-inspired robot movements. Furthermore, the multi-segment models generated by the binary search algorithm matched the ground truth models obtained through dynamic programming in over 97% of cases, and on average, contained one fewer segment than those produced by the Ramer–Douglas–Peucker algorithm, which is widely used in curvature simplification tasks. Our findings suggest that the binary search algorithm provides a computationally efficient approach for generating compact kinematic models and may facilitate the analysis of large datasets with high temporal and spatial resolution.

title: Estimation of cercospora leaf spot disease severity in table beets from UAS multispectral images
abstract: Cercospora leaf spot (CLS), caused by the fungus Cercospora beticola Sacc., is a severe foliar disease that affects the health of table beet crops. Remote sensing techniques, specifically unmanned aerial systems (UAS), could offer a valuable solution for evaluating disease progression and targeted fungicide application towards effectively managing CLS. We conducted UAS flights over C. beticola inoculated table beet plots at Cornell Agritech in Geneva, NY, USA during the growing seasons of 2021, 2022 and 2023. Five-band (475,560, 668, 717 and 840 nm) multispectral imagery was collected for the 2021 and 2022 flights, while for 2023 flights, a four-band (560, 650, 730 and 860 nm) sensor was used. CLS disease severity was assessed in situ at regular intervals, severity was evaluated using both spectral and textural features. Vegetation indices, derived from multispectral imagery, are known to be effective in assessing plant health and disease determination. Texture features also have been reported to be effective in determining plant traits since they provide additional pixel-spatial information to the model. Extensive selection was used to obtain the most relevant features. Our best-performing machine learning model used a random forest regressor to estimate disease severity at an R2test = 0.82 and RMSEtest = 9.31%. Furthermore, the disease progression was tracked using area-under-disease- progression-stairs (AUDPS) and the predicted values had a correlation coefficient of 0.84, 0.94 and 0.81 with 2021, 2022 and 2023 data, respectively. These results are strongly encouraging to support table beet growers with advanced data collection and analysis methodologies, enabling them to implement rapid and efficient foliar disease management strategies.

title: Editorial Board
FLARE: Focused leaf–lesion awareness via explicit relational modeling for field disease severity assessment
abstract: Plant leaf disease severity assessment can assist in quantifying the progression of the disease, providing a basis for precise pesticide application, which in turn effectively enhances crop production. Field disease assessment is usually confronted with complex background disturbances, making it difficult for previous methods that primarily rely on hybrid perception to explicitly and independently recognize lesion and leaf regions. The resulting information entanglement introduces bias into severity assessment and ultimately limits the applicability of such methods in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we propose a focused leaf–lesion awareness via explicit relational modeling (FLARE) for disease severity assessment. The proposed framework comprises two main components: a focused leaf–lesion awareness network (FLLA-Net) and an explicit relational modeling assessment network (ERMA-Net). The FLLA-Net utilizes lesion and leaf masks to guide the network’s focus on key regions. The resulting pretrained vision awareness extraction module (VAE-Module) is separately aware of prior visual knowledge of lesions and leaves, providing focused visual features for ERMA-Net. The ERMA-Net shares and freezes the parameters of the VAE-Module to extract hierarchical representations of lesions and leaves explicitly. It then performs a vision relational modeling module (VRM-Module) to simulate the distribution of lesions on leaves. The resulting relational features are refined through a global feature refinement block. A reinforcement-guided contrastive learning strategy is then incorporated to enrich semantic information, followed by a multi-layer perceptron for predicting disease severity levels. During inference, FLARE requires only images, enabling efficient and practical deployment in real-world scenarios. To support real-world applicability, we construct a comprehensive dataset of complex scenes with categories, segmentation masks, severity labels, and corresponding textual annotations. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves at least a 3.34% improvement in severity prediction accuracy compared to existing assessment models, confirming the effectiveness and practical potential of FLARE for disease severity assessment. Our code and dataset are available at http://flare.samlab.cn/.

title: Improving wheat yield prediction in breeding under climate change via a new method of correcting and reconstructing meteorological data and weighing multiple crop model outputs
abstract: Climate change increasingly affects wheat growth, yield, and quality, making accurate yield prediction essential for breeding climate-resilient crops. This study proposes a new prediction method to assess the impact of climate change on the yield of various wheat germplasms, experimentally carried out in Zhejiang Province, China. The method integrates a multivariable correction super-resolution diffusion model (MCSDM) and a multiple crop model weight distribution network (MCMWDN). First, MCSDM corrects and reconstructs daily historical and future meteorological data from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 multiple global climate models (GCMs). Then, crop models (WOFOST, AquaCrop, and DSSAT) were driven using corrected and reconstructed historical meteorological data to complete model calibration and validation. Finally, corrected and reconstructed future meteorological data were used to drive the calibrated and validated crop models, and the outputs of multiple crop models were integrated using MCMWDN to obtain future yield predictions for different wheat breeding germplasms under climate change. The results showed that the R2 of all seven GCM variables increased and the RMSE decreased under different future scenarios. MCMWDN integrated the outputs of multiple crop models, resulting in more accurate yield predictions (R2 = 0.823, RMSE = 443.6 kg/ha), which is superior to single crop models. Results show significant variation in the responses of different wheat germplasms to future climate scenarios. Norin 61 maintains relatively high yields, while Festin and Jagger/W94-244–132 perform poorly. Lumai 5 and Zhoumai 31 remain relatively stable overall. Yields tend to increase slightly under SSP1-2.6, stay stable under SSP2-4.5, and decline under SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5, especially by 2071–2100. This study provides a relatively robust and generalizable method for predicting crop yields, supporting climate-resilient breeding and management decisions for sustainable agriculture in the face of climate change.

title: Multi-strategy improved NSGA-II for light and nitrogen synergistic regulation of tomato seedlings to optimize resource use efficiency
abstract: Intelligent regulation in controlled environment agriculture is vital for photosynthesis and sustainability. However, balancing productivity with energy efficiency remains challenged by the limited convergence and solution diversity of conventional optimization methods. This work developed a multi-objective optimization framework combining Quantum Particle Swarm Optimization with a multi-strategy improved Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm-II (NSGA-II) for synergistic regulation of light intensity and the ammonium-nitrate ratio (NAR). Firstly, nested experiments were conducted to measure photosynthetic rate (Pn) of tomato seedlings under varying environmental conditions, and the constructed Pn prediction model achieved high accuracy with an R2 of 0.9745 and an RMSE of 0.0479 μmol · m−2·s−1. Then, this study quantified photosynthesis and light use efficiency (LUE) in regulation process and formulated this problem as a multi-objective optimization problem. The good point set initialization, diversity preservation guided by variance, and refined elitism strategy were employed to improve NSGA-II, effectively improving the solution diversity and convergence of the standard NSGA-II. The results showed that the proposed approach maintained approximately 92.61% of Pn compared with maximum Pn light supplementation method, while achieving a significant reduction of 44.22% in photosynthetic photon flux density and more than doubling the average LUE. Finally, a growth validation experiment tested the optimized regulation strategy. The test results showed that the proposed regulation approach more than doubled root dry weight, whole fresh weight and the health index compared with fixed NAR method. This work provided an effective framework for the synergistic optimization of light and nutrient inputs in plant seedling systems, ensuring efficient agricultural production and resource utilization.

title: Event triggered disturbance observer based nonlinear MPC for agricultural machinery trajectory tracking control
abstract: Autonomous operation of agricultural machinery in uneven and slippery terrain necessitates highly accurate trajectory tracking control. While Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) provides a robust formulation for this task, its real-time implementation is often limited by high computational demands, model uncertainties, and time-varying external disturbances. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel event-triggered disturbance observer based NMPC framework for agricultural machinery trajectory tracking to enhance tracking performance while reducing computational time. A nonlinear disturbance observer integrated with an Actor–Critic Neural Network (ACNN) is developed to dynamically estimate and compensate for both model uncertainties and time-varying external disturbances. A novel Pseudo-Huber cost function is utilized to formulate a dynamically smooth input saturation model to manage actuator constraints and prevent saturation-induced instability. To further reduce computational overhead, an event-triggered mechanism is implemented, where optimization updates are activated only when the prediction error between the system’s optimal forecasted state and its actual measured state exceeds a predefined threshold. This mechanism reduces the frequency of optimization computations, thereby alleviating the computational burden inherent in conventional NMPC, without compromising control performance. Comprehensive simulations are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed control scheme. The results demonstrate that the event-triggered disturbance observer based NMPC method not only achieves substantial savings in computational resources compared to NMPC but also maintains high trajectory tracking accuracy under the influence of disturbances.

title: A shuffle-normalized Pix2Pix GAN framework with Elastic ArcFace and YOLO for occlusion-free cattle identification
abstract: In recent years, biometric-based cattle identification, particularly using muzzle patterns, has emerged as a reliable and non-invasive solution. However, real-world muzzle images often suffer from occlusions caused by grass, dirt, and environmental noise, which adversely affect identification performance. Generative Adversarial Networks, especially Pix2Pix GAN, offer a promising approach for translating noisy images into clean, realistic representations. Nevertheless, GAN training is challenging due to instability and mode collapse. Traditional normalization techniques like Batch Normalization provide limited benefits, as they fail to fully exploit the architectural characteristics of GANs. To address these issues, this work proposes a novel normalization technique called Shuffle Normalization, integrated into the Pix2Pix GAN framework for generating clean muzzle images from noisy inputs. Shuffle Normalization improves training stability and image quality by preserving semantic information and mitigating gradient saturation. For cattle identification, an Elastic Face Margin Loss-based classifier is employed, trained on real muzzle images and evaluated using GAN-generated outputs. The proposed method achieves a Frechet Inception Distance score of 13.92, indicating high visual fidelity of the generated images, and an identification accuracy of 98.7%, demonstrating the effectiveness of the overall framework. This work advances generative modeling in animal biometrics and provides a robust solution for real-world cattle identification, while also establishing a practical generative AI–based paradigm for occlusion-robust data augmentation and biometric recognition in precision livestock farming.

title: A CNN-LSTM-based feature-level generation model for detecting the degree of salt stress in soybeans
abstract: Soybean is one of the most important crops globally as an oil crop and a key source of plant protein. Salt stress caused by soil salinization has become a significant factor affecting soybean yield. This paper proposes a feature-level generative model based on CNN-LSTM. Rather than generating images, the model directly generates corresponding fluorescence features from the RGB features of soybean seedling leaves extracted by the CNN. These generated features are combined with the RGB features to accurately detect the degree of salt stress. The results show that combining RGB features with generated Y(NO) fluorescence features achieves a detection accuracy of 97.30%, surpassing the accuracy of using only RGB and even outperforming the combination of RGB with actual Y(NO) fluorescence features. This method reduces the need for fluorescence image acquisition, thereby lowering the cost and complexity of data collection. It provides an efficient and cost-effective solution for the early detection of salt stress in soybeans.

title: Behavior recognition and abnormality detection for Muscovy ducks under various lighting conditions using an IoT-Based system
abstract: The proposed system is based on an IoT-controlled lighting platform and enables real-time monitoring of poultry behavior under different illumination conditions. By integrating an IoT-based environmental control system with an improved deep learning model (DBR-YOLOv8), the proposed framework enables long-term behavioral data collection under multiple illumination conditions and provides intuitive interpretability through heatmap visualization and statistical analysis, thereby reducing the difficulty of manual observation in complex lighting environments. Using the IoT platform, lighting parameters including illuminance, exposure duration, and spectral configuration were precisely controlled, while video data were recorded. Under regular light, simulated sunlight, spectral variation, and dark night conditions, DBR-YOLOv8 achieved mAP values of 92.0%, 93.4%, 96.1%, and 95.8%, respectively, demonstrating robust behavior recognition performance across variable lighting environments. Based on data collected from 180 Muscovy ducks and over 18 million images across a multi-group, replicated experimental design involving 18 housing units, the system further enabled quantitative analysis of four abnormal behaviors. The results indicated that light duration, high-intensity exposure time, illumination intensity, and spectral variation significantly influenced abnormal behavior frequency. In particular, regression analysis suggested a 4-hour high-intensity period at 3000 lx with a simulated sunlight spectrum as a prioritized candidate configuration associated with reduced abnormal behavior expression.

title: Agrosense v2: An AI-enabled system for precision orchard sensing and tree-level monitoring
abstract: Precision orchard management requires robust sensing systems that operate reliably under unstructured field conditions while providing actionable, tree-level information. Despite advances in computer vision and edge computing, most approaches focus on isolated tasks and lack integration into deployable, orchard-scale systems. This study presents Next-Generation Agrosense (Agrosense v2), an AI-enabled, system-oriented framework for real-time orchard sensing and tree-level monitoring. Agrosense v2 integrates tree detection and counting, canopy density classification, tree height estimation (inherited from Agrosense v1, not validated in detail in this study), and detection-based fruit counting on both the tree and the ground into a unified pipeline. Compared with the previous version (Agrosense v1), Agrosense v2 improves tree identification through temporal tracking, strengthens canopy density classification by leveraging image sequences, and adds fruit counting via image-level detection, with all outputs aggregated into tree-level spatiotemporal summaries, presented by a self-developed tree-level visualization tool. Field experiments in three citrus orchards with contrasting management conditions totaled 3,696 trees across two commercial orchards (Field A&B) and a research station (SWFREC). Tree counting accuracies were 95.96% (SWFREC), 92.73% (Field A), and 97.79% (Field B), and canopy density classification accuracies were 94.1% to 96.8%. For fruit detection, the transformer-based RT-DETR model achieved the highest mAP@0.5 up to 0.837 and 0.722 for fruits on the tree and ground, respectively, demonstrating robustness under dense canopy and cluttered ground conditions. To our knowledge, Agrosense v2 is the first real-time, field-deployable orchard sensing system that delivers multiple tree-level attributes within a single framework. By unifying perception, inference, and geo-referenced aggregation, Agrosense v2 provides a scalable foundation for data-driven precision orchard management.

title: Detecting potato leafhopper infestation in beans using hyperspectral leaf-level sensing
abstract: Potato leafhopper (PLH; Empoasca fabae Harris) is a sap-feeding pest known for its wide host range and high damage potential. Although known to cause significant yield losses across agricultural commodities including beans, spectral signatures of PLH induced stress in beans have not yet been explored. To address this gap, a greenhouse study was conducted to evaluate the capability of hyperspectral reflectance sensing in detecting PLH stress. Specifically, the study aimed to characterize hyperspectral responses of PLH stress in beans, assess the effects of infestation density and duration, and identify consistent stress-sensitive spectral regions across bean varieties. The study included three bean varieties- Provider (Phaseolus vulgaris), Henderson’s Bush Lima (Phaseolus lunatus), and Tiger’s Eye (Phaseolus vulgaris)- where beans were subjected to varying densities and durations of PLH infestation. Generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) with cubic regression splines were employed to capture the non-linear wavelength-specific reflectance responses on beans under varying PLH infestation. Pairwise differences among the infestation-specific smooths were calculated to identify spectral regions (500–1000 nm) where reflectance differed significantly. Results of the study identified, for each variety, spectral regions within the visible and near-infrared (NIR) spectrum where leaf reflectance differed among the healthy and infested beans. Results revealed that PLH feeding stress induced distinct, wavelength-specific and variety-dependent reflectance shifts across the spectrum. With increased infestation duration, reflectance differences were evident across broader spectral regions of the visible and NIR spectrum, although the magnitude and direction of reflectance responses varied among varieties. Provider and Henderson’s Bush Lima exhibited pronounced spectral separation with increasing infestation duration, while Tiger’s Eye showed delayed response, requiring higher infestation pressure for clear differentiation. These findings provide the first evidence that PLH-induced feeding damage in beans can be detected using leaf reflectance, offering a novel reflectance-based approach for monitoring crop stress caused by PLH. The study establishes a foundation for developing reflectance-based tools for early detection and scalable monitoring of PLH stress in precision agriculture.

title: Slide-DQN: Adaptive slip control for crawler agricultural machinery in hilly and mountainous terrains using modified deep Q-network
abstract: Maintaining driving stability control in crawler agricultural machinery under non-stationary operating conditions in hilly and mountainous terrain remains challenging due to strong nonlinearities, continuous time-varying uncertainties, and unpredictable dynamics. Existing approaches lack robust models for instability prediction under soil texture fluctuations, and the compensation mechanisms of drive control systems remain inadequately characterized, hindering optimal torque distribution between tracks. This study proposes Slide-DQN, an adaptive slip control method based on a modified Deep Q-Network (DQN). The approach features targeted designs of the state-action space, neural network architecture, and reward function. Slide-DQN is integrated with the pure pursuit navigation algorithm to achieve adaptive navigation and slip control. Experimental validation was conducted using a crawler slip experiment platform. Results demonstrate that in adaptive navigation control experiments under Scene N2, the maximum tracking deviation decreased by 75.0% and over-correction distance was reduced by 40.0%. Under Scene N9, maximum deviation decreased by 70.6% and over-correction distance was reduced by 55.6%. These results validate the algorithm’s superiority in enhancing trajectory tracking stability during slip conditions in hilly and mountainous terrains, significantly improving navigation accuracy.

title: Combination of metric-based few-shot and contrastive learning for soybean high-throughput phenotype under high temperature stress
abstract: Soybeans play a crucial role in global food security, and the increasing severity of heat stress due to climate change in recent years has highlighted the growing importance of phenotypic assessment for breeding. While unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) remote sensing offers a low-cost, high-throughput, and non-destructive approach for canopy phenotyping, variations among soybean genotypes and across growing seasons lead to scarce labeled data, which limits the applicability of traditional deep learning models. This study aims to develop a novel few-shot learning algorithm for identifying soybean canopy phenotypes under high-temperature stress (HT) and control (CK) conditions, utilizing two years of UAV RGB and near-infrared (NIR) imagery. This study proposes the Soybean Contrastive Prototypical Network (SCProtoNet), a metric-based few-shot learning model designed for accurate phenotypic analysis of soybean canopies. Specifically, SCProtoNet employs a dual-branch architecture to jointly process RGB and NIR images, effectively capturing phenotypic differences in soybean canopies caused by genotypes by optimizing prototype representations and contrastive learning instance discrimination based on few-shot scenarios. As a result, in the first year, SCProtoNet achieves an accuracy of 91.56% in a 1-shot training setting. In the second year, weights transferred from the first year are used to validate the generalization performance of the model across experimental years. Retraining the model in a 16-shot setting achieves experimental results of 87.65% and 100%. This few-shot learning model has been effectively tested on canopy images of 3232 different soybean genotypes. Experimental results demonstrate the robustness and generalization performance of the model across different experimental periods. SCProtoNet provides a valuable reference for implementing soybean genotype selection and lays the foundation for phenotypic analysis tasks in other crops under few-shot conditions. The source code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Lzylearn/SCProtoNet-Soybean.

title: A temperature correction strategy for leaf spectral data to improve the estimation of leaf nitrogen concentration, leaf mass per area and carbon
abstract: Variations in leaf temperature can introduce significant confounding effects in leaf spectral reflectance data, thereby complicating the accurate retrieval of physiological traits. To mitigate this issue, a temperature correction strategy that minimizes spectral differences across datasets was developed. The method derives an average reflectance distance metric based on loading space standardization (LSS), which is subsequently linked to the quadratic term of temperature. This distance indicator, combined with variable importance in projection (VIP) scores, corrects spectral data effectively. Following correction, sample disparities were substantially reduced in all five independent datasets. The temperature-corrected spectra, particularly within the Visible and Near-Infrared (NIR) regions, demonstrated an enhanced contribution to the estimation of leaf nitrogen concentration (LNC), leaf mass per area (LMA), and Carbon content. The performance of four regression models (partial least squares-PLS, support vector regression-SVR, extreme gradient boosting-XGB, and random forest regression-RFR) was evaluated using temperature-corrected spectra. Model robustness was assessed via 10-fold cross-validation and independent testing. The results indicate a consistent improvement in estimation performance post-correction. Specifically, the RFR model achieved the highest accuracy, with average root mean square error (RMSE) reductions of 12.9% for LNC, 11.3% for LMA, and 10.3% for Carbon. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis revealed that key spectral bands in Visible, NIR, and Short-Wave Infrared (SWIR) regions consistently ranked among the top 10 influential variables after correction. Furthermore, synergistic interactions among these bands were identified, aligning with established spectral characteristics of the targeted biochemical constituents. The principal novelty of this work lies in the integration of LSS with VIP scores for temperature correction, which effectively addresses spectral variations across different samples and temperature conditions. The validated prediction performance of the models underscores the utility of the proposed temperature correction framework for improving the robustness of spectral trait estimation.

title: Assessment of spectrogram correlation, eigensounds, and YAMNet embeddings in detecting cattle vocalizations
abstract: Acoustic monitoring enables unattended health and welfare surveillance in Precision Livestock Farming (PLF). This study reports practical insights from developing and field-testing a prototype system at an experimental farm. We used recordings from twenty Holstein multiparous lactating dairy cows, each monitored individually in a tied stanchion barn, with temporary isolation of 4 hours post-morning milkings to facilitate data capture. We compared three approaches for automatic detection of cattle vocalisations: (1) spectrogram cross-correlation using Praat and Parselmouth, (2) an eigensounds method based on Principal Component Analysis, and (3) embedding similarity using the pre-trained YAMNet model. On a curated set of twenty 1-hour recordings collected from isolated pens, the correlation method achieved rather modest results, with only three recordings achieving an F1-score above 0.5. With suitable component counts and thresholds, the eigensounds approach yielded moderate results, with half of the recordings achieving an F1-score above 0.5, but high inter-individual variability, as adjusting thresholds improves precision for some subjects but greatly reduces recall for others. YAMNet achieved consistently high precision, with recall adjustable through thresholding and template selection, even under considerable noise. We further examine how thresholding and event capping influence precision–recall performance, and we outline a semi-automated labeling workflow, discussing the potential of wearable recorders and other strategies to enhance accuracy.

title: In situ orange soluble solids content estimation based on hyperspectral imaging and transformer
abstract: The in-field estimation of the oranges’ soluble solids content (SSC) using hyperspectral imaging(HSI) holds significant importance in facilitating the implementation of automated agricultural robots for selective harvesting operations and ensure the fruit quality. However, HSI analysis primarily utilizes the conventional machine learning approaches trained on small-scale datasets, which restricts prediction accuracy and generalization capability. Additionally, the high cost of hyperspectral cameras greatly hampers their widespread application in agricultural scenarios. This study proposed the utilization of transformer-based models for HSI analysis to SSC of oranges. Moreover, it explored the use of spectral reconstruction algorithms in reconstructing hyperspectral images from RGB images. A dataset for citrus was first established, which comprises 1536 samples; each sample includes a hyperspectral image, a RGB image and its corresponding SSC value, collected the growth of citrus from early maturity to late harvest across various field conditions. The hyperspectral images without reflectance calibration and dimensional reduction were utilized as input for training the transformer-based model for SSC prediction. The proposed transformer-based SSC prediction model on raw data demonstrated 14.8% better performance than PLS in terms of R2 (0.70 vs. 0.61), 11.7% better in terms of RMSE (0.83°Brix vs. 0.94°Brix). To validate the effectiveness of spectral reconstruction models, reconstructed hyperspectral images from RGB images are used for estimating the SSC of oranges. Their SSC prediction results consistently outperformed those derived from the corresponding RGB images, whether these were rendered from hyperspectral images (R2 = 0.64 vs. 0.56) or captured using a smartphone RGB sensor (R2 = 0.48 vs. 0.42). These results indicated that the capabilities of deep learning technologies to reduce costs and enhance accuracy, which can help promote the widespread application of automated selective harvesting operations and ripeness monitoring in agricultural scenarios.

title: A truss-type field phenotyping platform combining Beidou georeferencing for in-situ monitoring of individual rapeseed in multi-growth stage
abstract: Automatic collection of multi-temporal phenotypic traits in field-grown rapeseed is essential for modern breeding but remains difficult under dense planting and canopy overlap. A truss-type phenotyping platform integrating Beidou georeferencing with RGB, LiDAR, and multispectral sensors has been developed to achieve precise, cost-effective, and efficient in-situ monitoring of individual plants. A plant centroid localization method based on YOLOv11n achieved an average precision of 88.2% and a mean localization error of 9.3 pixels (approximately 0.011 m). Plant height extraction from point clouds reached centimeter-level accuracy and correlated well with manual measurements (R2 = 0.9498, RMSE = 0.0217 m, MAE = 0.0196 m, RPD = 3.6360). In terms of efficiency, processing one plot containing 30 plants (1.2 MB, 80,000 points) required about 4 s. Platform validation demonstrated positioning accuracy of 0.02 m and reliable motion control with an average delay of 36.1 ms. Compared with commercial truss systems, the proposed platform reduced costs by more than 80% while maintaining high accuracy and throughput. These results highlight its potential as a practical tool for large-scale breeding trials in rapeseed and other dense crops.

title: Image-Based, 3D reconstruction for smart farming Applications: A review
abstract: As a core driving force in the digital transformation of smart farming, 3D reconstruction technology has recently been shown to have substantial potential for agricultural environmental perception, precision operations, and decision-making support. This review summarizes recent advances in image-based 3D reconstruction from both methodological and application perspectives. Conventional methods, including voxel carving, Structure from Motion and Multi-View Stereo (SfM-MVS), and photometric stereo, are first reviewed, followed by recent developments in deep learning–based reconstruction, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). These methods are discussed in relation to the major challenges of agricultural environments, including occlusion, heterogeneous illumination, and target motion. Representative applications in crop phenotyping, robotic perception and operation, and livestock monitoring are then analyzed, with comparison of technical systems in terms of accuracy, cost, and adaptability. Finally, current limitations related to real-time performance, robustness, and system integration are discussed, and future directions in lightweight modeling, multimodal data fusion, and edge deployment are outlined.

title: Towards standardised measurement of ammonia emissions from naturally ventilated dairy barns: Progress and perspectives
abstract: • Measuring NH 3 emissions in naturally ventilated barns is a significant challenge. • Barn structure, ventilation rate and pollutant dispersion are sources of uncertainty. • NH 3 emission factor in naturally ventilated barns depends on sampling strategies. • CO 2 mass balance and direct airflow measurements are the most common methods. • Modelling tools may complement experimental measurements and support data interpretation. Measuring ammonia (NH 3 ) emissions from naturally ventilated dairy barns (NVBs) is a significant challenge due to their structural heterogeneity, dynamic and variable airflow, and complex pollutant dispersion. However, these emissions contribute to air pollution, ecosystem acidification, and eutrophication. Accurate quantification is essential for complying with regulations and implementing effective mitigation strategies, but it is complicated by variable climate conditions and the lack of shared international measurement standards. The study critically analyses progress in measuring NH 3 emissions from NVBs through a critical review based on a systematic literature search in recent years, assessing the state of method consolidation, identifying emerging approaches, investigating critical issues related to measurement uncertainty, and highlighting the growing interest in advanced tools to support data interpretation. The review was conducted using the Scopus and Web of Science databases, and the final dataset was subjected to critical analysis, including categorising the methods, objectives, and main topics, and examining emission factors, uncertainty, and modelling. The results highlight a progressive methodological convergence on CO 2 mass balance and direct airflow measurements as the most common strategies for quantifying emissions. The analysis of emission factors (EFs) showed values ranging from 0 to 2.4 g h −1 LU -1 , with variability across studies. Clear seasonal differences were observed, with higher EF values consistently reported during summer, while additional variability was associated with differences in sampling strategies. Despite the inherent complexity of NVBs, methodological advances in recent years have improved the ability to quantify, predict, and correct uncertainties in NH 3 emissions.

title: Few-shot crop mapping via nonlinear representation equilibrium network
abstract: Few-shot learning (FSL) effectively solves the problem of high annotation cost commonly in crop mapping with hyperspectral imagery (HSI). However, there are also some challenges, including limited class generalization and the difficulty in representing high-dimensional spectral data. To address these problems, we proposed the Nonlinear Representation Equilibrium Network (NR-ENet). The network first incorporated an Equilibrium Data Augmentation (EDA) strategy to enhance the contribution of underrepresented classes and to construct multi-scale spatial–spectral windows. Then, a Spectral Feature Extractor (SFE) was employed to capture stable nonlinear features, and a Local Spectral Selector (LSS) was designed to filter redundant information and extract discriminative spectral features. Experimental results demonstrated that the classification accuracy of NR-ENet reached 88.02%, 11.76% higher than the existing methods. These findings suggest that NR-ENet provides a data-efficient and robust solution for crop hyperspectral mapping under limited-label conditions.

title: From individual identification to behavioral sensing—evolution and challenges of RFID technology in precision livestock farming
abstract: Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) faces an urgent demand for the automated and fine-grained monitoring of individual animals within large-scale herds. Radio Frequency Identification (RFID), characterized by its contactless and automated capabilities, has emerged as a cornerstone technology addressing this need. This paper systematically reviews the application evolution of RFID in PLF and proposes a novel four-stage evolutionary framework transitioning from “identification” to “sensing.” The framework details the technological progression from basic individual and group identification via near/far-field communication, to macro-behavioral analysis based on ID temporal sequences, and finally to fine-grained tracking and micro-physiological sensing leveraging physical layer signals such as Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) and Phase. Furthermore, the review synthesizes core challenges regarding sensing accuracy, hardware performance, data standardization, and implementation costs. To address these, strategies such as hardware-software co-optimization, multi-modal fusion, and the establishment of data standards are proposed. Looking forward, the potential of RFID extends beyond the individual level: by analyzing spatio-temporal co-occurrence relationships, it can decode complex social behaviors in herds. Furthermore, deep mining of physical layer signals presents the theoretical potential for passive physiological sensing (e.g., heart rate and respiration), though substantial in-vivo validation remains necessary. Ultimately, the review identifies the ’RFID+’ ecosystem as the critical trajectory: utilizing RFID as the core hub to anchor identity across multi-modal data, thereby facilitating a highly integrated and intelligent perception network for PLF.

title: Real-time detection method for corn seed spacing and sowing rate based on the seed identity matching rule
abstract: Precise detection of seed spacing and sowing rate is essential for evaluating the quality of mechanized corn planting. To address this, we propose a real-time detection method based on an improved YOLOv8 model and a Seed Identity Matching Rule. The proposed method integrates a Slim-neck lightweight architecture and C2f-EMA enhanced feature extraction module into YOLOv8 to optimize seed detection efficiency. Additionally, a Seed Identity Matching Rule was developed to eliminate duplicate counting across consecutive frames, enabling precise calculation of seed spacing and sowing rates. The improved YOLOv8 model achieves optimal performance: the inference speed is 73 FPS and only 5.1 MB. The mAP@50:95 reaches 81.33%, which is 14.2 points improvement over the original model. Bench testing on a KINZE T4000 yielded an average sowing rate error of 3.9% across rotation speeds of 20–60 rpm. Further validation on a JPS-12 test bench showed a seed spacing Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.55 cm with a Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of 0.99. In field experiments, the method demonstrated high robustness, achieving a seed spacing MAE of 1.25 cm and a PCC of 0.99. These results confirm the method’s reliability for real-time performance evaluation and adaptive control in high-precision, high-speed planters.

title: An innovative UWB-based RTLS robot for autonomous barn cleaning in smart farming
abstract: This paper presents the development and implementation of a robot prototype whose function is to automate the alleys cleaning operations within a barn, thus facilitating human labour. This robot moves into the barn according to sensors installed both on the robot itself and on the ceiling, so as to complete the trajectory it has to follow for cleaning operations; this is what makes this system a Real Time Locating System (RTLS), since the robot is mainly driven according to the sensors positioned inside the barn ceiling. The function of this robot, provided with ad hoc arms, is that of cleaning the area by converging and collecting cows’ manure. This manure is supposed to be re-used as fertilizer for the cultivated areas of the farm. The RTLS system in question is based on a commercial radio indoor positioning system, which leverages Ultra-Wide Band radio frequency to determine the exact position of the tags installed on the robot, so as to guide it. The barn selected for the implementation of this system is located in Parma, Northern Italy. The system shows higher accuracy than comparable solutions, with an average localization error of 0.30 m in the selected scenario. This project represents a novelty, since RTLS applications in the agri-food context are almost nil, and a similar solution does not exist.

title: Risk-controlled adaptive local calibration for NIRS-based nutrient prediction in liquid organic manure
abstract: Accurate quantification of nutrients in liquid organic manure (LOM) is critical for precision agriculture at field application. Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) provides a rapid, non-destructive approach for this analysis. However, predictive accuracy strongly depends on the chosen calibration regime. Global calibration models use the entire training dataset to capture overall data structure, but their performance may decline under substantial compositional heterogeneity. In contrast, local calibration variants restrict model fitting to spectrally similar reference samples, introducing additional flexibility but also increased variance sensitivity. This study systematically examines structural heterogeneity in NIRS-based LOM datasets and compares multiple neighborhood-based local model variants to a global partial least squares regression (PLSR) baseline. Oracle analysis demonstrates that no single locality regime is uniformly optimal across samples or nutrients, revealing pronounced sample-dependent suitability across local model families representing distinct locality regimes. To address this heterogeneity, family-level selection is formulated as a learning-to-rank problem. A margin-based gating policy activates local model families only when their predicted utility exceeds a predefined risk budget, enabling explicit control over performance degradation relative to the global reference. For four nutrients, the proposed framework achieves high ranking fidelity (nDCG > 0.90) and deployable performance gains of up to Δ AE = 0 . 19 , while maintaining an empirical worsen rate below 5%. Improvements concentrate in high-error regimes of the global model, indicating targeted allocation of modeling complexity rather than indiscriminate model switching. The results establish risk-controlled adaptive local calibration for heterogeneous agricultural NIRS applications and demonstrate its potential for nutrient monitoring within precision fertilization workflows.

title: Two-way FSI modelling and validation of wind-induced mechanical damage on maize under quadrotor UAV downwash
abstract: Stronger UAV downwash can enhance maize canopy penetration but also increases turbulent loading, which can induce stalk bending and leaf breakage, thereby reducing yield and quality. To characterise this trade-off, this study developed a two-way fluid–structure interaction (FSI) model coupling quadrotor downwash with the maize plant. Simulations covered flight heights of 2–6 m and forward speeds of 2–6 m/s, together with over-canopy hovering and lateral hovering. Plant responses (displacement, stress/strain, and absorbed energy) were quantified, and a damage index (DI) was established for risk-informed parameter screening. The results showed that operating state markedly altered downwash intensity and structure: low height/low speed and hovering intensified near-canopy loading, while lateral hovering and forward flight promoted a downwash-wake pattern that produced asymmetric forcing, mid-to-lower leaf deflection, and unilateral stalk bending. Mechanically vulnerable regions were concentrated at the stalk base, the leaf-stalk junction, and the mid-to-upper leaf lamina. The tendency for lodging was primarily governed by the leaf alignment plane because of its greater aerodynamic torque. Model predictions agreed well with measurements, with mean relative errors of 14.51% for wind speed, 11.83% for stress, and 9.48% for displacement. In dynamic validation, the coefficients of determination for both leaf-tip displacement and stem bending in the YZ plane exceeded 0.85. Overall, a risk-constrained operating envelope of 4–6 m height and forward speed ≥ 4 m/s, while minimising hovering, especially lateral hovering, is recommended to balance application efficiency and crop mechanical safety.

title: Authentication and adulteration detection of true cinnamon (Cinnamomum zeylanicum) essential oil using an integrated multi-analytical and electronic nose approach
abstract: Food adulteration poses a critical challenge to food security, affordability, and consumer trust, particularly for high-value food ingredients traded in global supply chains. Addressing adulteration in true cinnamon ( Cinnamomum zeylanicum ) essential oil, a premium product whose authenticity directly impacts economic accessibility and fair market practices, this study employed a multi-analytical approach, integrating an electronic nose (e-nose) combined with chemometric tools, physicochemical, chromatographic, and spectroscopic analyses. The aim of this work was to authenticate true cinnamon oil and to discriminate samples according to adulterant type and concentration, demonstrating the potential of digital sensing systems for rapid food authenticity verification and affordability protection. Samples were prepared by of intentionally adulterating the pure oil with vaseline, false cinnamon ( Cinnamomum cassia ) oil, and vegetable oils (corn, soybean, and sunflower) at varying concentrations (0 to 100%). The authenticity of the essential oils (EOs) was first confirmed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC–MS), which showed cinnamaldehyde contents of 78.6% in true cinnamon bark essential oil (TCBEO) and only 42.3% in false cinnamon bark essential oil (FCBEO). Physicochemical analyses (density, refractive index, optical rotation, and solubility in ethanol) revealed deviations above 20% in adulterated samples compared to pure oil. ATR-FTIR spectroscopy identified marker bands of cinnamaldehyde at 1666–1613 cm⁻ 1 (C=O) and eugenol at 1124 cm −1 (C–O), whose intensities decreased proportionally with adulteration, while triglyceride bands (∼1740 cm −1 ) increased. The poly (lactic acid)/poly(ethylene glycol) (PLA/PEG) substrate of gas sensors (S3 and S4) exhibited the highest response. At 75% adulteration, S4 showed a ΔR/R 0 1.2x higher than S1 and 1.8x higher than S2, indicating enhanced efficiency. Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) classification achieved accuracies above 92% for all adulterants and up to 99.95% for FCBEO adulteration. The integration of GC–MS, physicochemical analysis, ATR-FTIR, and e-nose sensing demonstrates a scalable, rapid, and cost-effective digital approach to food authenticity control, supporting resilient and affordable food systems.

title: Official tests of MFWD tractors based on wheel force transducers and validation of tractor performance prediction model
abstract: Verifying the internal inter-axle coupling mechanism of Mechanical-Front Wheel Drive (MFWD) tractors remains a critical challenge in terramechanics. Conventional validation methods, which rely on total drawbar pull, effectively act as a “black box,” unable to isolate the specific force contributions of front and rear tires and directly quantify the “push-pull” effect. To overcome this experimental opacity and provide a rigorous theoretical explanation, this study introduces a rigorous “white-box” validation framework that integrates a transparent analytical model with high-fidelity experimental decoupling. Grounded in a modular tire-soil sub-model, the framework explicitly integrates dynamic tire load distribution with the inter-axle kinematic coupling mechanism. To address the multivariate and nonlinear nature of the system, a prediction algorithm using a two-dimensional iterative method was designed. The core innovation lies in the experimental approach: six-component Wheel Force Transducers (WFT) were employed in official drawbar tests to decouple soil variability from vehicle dynamics. Crucially, the experiment provided direct, quantitative evidence of the “push-pull” effect, successfully capturing instances where the rear axle exhibited negative slip and longitudinal force while the front axle actively pulled—thereby verifying the hypothesis that internal force distribution results from the interaction between individual tire adhesion and inter-axle kinematic coupling. Experimental results demonstrate that the original (uncalibrated) model correctly captures the structural trends of inter-axle force distribution, confirming the physical validity of the derived analytical framework. Following coefficient optimization for local conditions, the model achieved high precision (approximately 1.0% error for drawbar pull in 4WD mode). This work proves that classic sub-models, when integrated into a correct system-level framework and verified by decoupled WFT measurements, remain highly effective for characterizing complex multi-axle dynamics, providing a robust foundation for precision machinery design.

title: Large-scale orange fruit dataset for localization, classification and ripening assessment under varying environments
abstract: The presented dataset is a large-scale on-field orange image collection designed for fruit detection, classification, and ripening assessment in real-world orchard environments. It includes 5025 images captured under diverse weather, lighting conditions, and ripening stages. Images were collected using different smartphone cameras and preprocessed through a custom cropping algorithm to optimize annotation efficiency. The dataset was labeled using a semi-automated approach, combining YOLO-based pre-annotations refined manually in Roboflow. Annotation quality was further improved through a CLIP-based verification process to filter incorrect labels. The dataset is released with both YOLO and COCO annotations, enabling compatibility with multiple object detection frameworks.
