Results demonstrate that this adaptive approach enhances production efficiency, yielding a projected revenue increase of up to 27.6%, representing a significant advancement in computational agriculture and offering a scalable solution for fully automated, profit-optimized insect farming.

title: Automated sea cage geometry detection from 3D multibeam sonar using machine learning
abstract: Reliable interpretation of acoustic observations in aquaculture systems requires accurate knowledge of the spatial structure being monitored. In flexible sea cages, geometric deformation under varying hydrodynamic conditions alters the spatial reference frame used to analyse sensor data and can lead to errors in automated monitoring and analysis. This study presents an automated, data-driven approach for detecting sea cage geometry directly from 3D multibeam sonar observations collected at a commercial salmon farm. The approach combines time-synchronised acoustic measurements with physics-based simulation-derived reference geometries and trains a 3D convolutional neural network to infer cage geometry from sonar data alone. The final implementation was developed in PyTorch using supervised training on matched sonar–geometry pairs. Validation results show strong agreement between predicted and reference cage geometries, with overlap-based similarity values in the range of approximately 0.93–0.94. These results demonstrate that cage geometry can be inferred directly from sonar observations without relying on external deformation sensors during operation. The proposed method provides a non-invasive and scalable approach for real-time cage-scale monitoring and supports downstream applications such as fish behaviour analysis, biomass interpretation, and precision aquaculture decision support.

title: Generative diffusion models for agricultural AI: Plant image generation, indoor-to-outdoor translation, and expert preference alignment
abstract: Agricultural AI is often constrained by limited, imbalanced plant image datasets and pronounced domain shift when models trained on controlled indoor imagery are deployed in field conditions. To address these challenges, we propose an integrated diffusion-based framework with three components that can be used independently or as complementary stages: (1) text-conditioned plant image synthesis to expand labeled training data, (2) indoor-to-outdoor image translation to mitigate domain shift, and (3) expert preference-aligned fine-tuning to improve agronomic realism and output stability. Our implementation builds on a Stable Diffusion v1.4 backbone fine-tuned with our domain-specific image dataset, which is then served as the base model for the image-translation module using the DreamBooth strategy. The fine-tuned generative model is further optimized by a reward-weighted mechanism using expert scores to refine image quality. We evaluate the framework using standard generative metrics (IS, FID) and downstream agricultural tasks, including phenotype classification and weed detection with YOLOv8. Results indicate that the components are synergistic: the synthesis model provides a strong initialization for translation, translation improves field realism while retaining utility for data augmentation, and preference alignment further enhances consistency and expert-perceived quality. Overall, the proposed framework offers a practical, data-efficient, and expert-aware generative pipeline for real-world agricultural AI.

title: Improving hyperspectral prediction accuracy of soil organic matter using Novel cascaded optimization methods and super ensemble model
abstract: Vis-NIR combined with the Stacking ensemble model (EM) has significant potential to enhance SOM prediction accuracy. However, existing Stacking EM research typically involves only one base learner and one meta-learner, making it difficult to capture internal feature connections in complex data. The diversity and complexity of base learners also lead to challenges in parameter tuning and can result in overfitting. Furthermore, local optimization consumes substantial computational resources and may trap EM in local optima. We hypothesize that incorporating base learners with varied performance levels allows each learner to better capture relationships within specific data subsets. This approach mitigates high value underestimation and low value overestimation in special value processing, enhancing EM’s overall robustness. This study utilizes 704 soil samples from the Tarim River Basin in Xinjiang, China, to develop a multi-level Super ensemble model (SEM) and an optimization strategy called Cascade Optimization (CO) to validate this hypothesis. The research findings indicate that, in comparison to traditional Stacking EM, the SEM we developed enhances the prediction accuracy of SOM, with R2 rising by 0.023 and RMSE dropping by 0.06 g kg−1. The SEM’s performance following CO overall optimization surpasses that after traditional local optimization, where R2 and RMSE improve by 0.032 and decrease by 0.20 g kg−1, respectively. Furthermore, CO significantly reduces computational resource consumption compared to traditional local optimization, with a 35.5% reduction in time complexity and a 30.8% reduction in space complexity. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the CO method and SEM. The ensemble of CO with SEM not only enhances the prediction accuracy of SOM but also substantially decreases computational resource consumption, offering theoretical backing for the rapid detection of SOM content and the practical application of near-end soil sensing.

title: Cypnet enabled spatiotemporal modeling of UAV hyperspectral imagery for wheat yield prediction and drought tolerant genotype identification
abstract: Accurate yield prediction and rapid identification of drought tolerant genotypes are critical for wheat breeding under increasing water scarcity. Despite recent advances in UAV based hyperspectral remote sensing and deep learning, a major unresolved challenge remains the robust modeling of high dimensional hyperspectral data across multiple phenological stages, particularly in large and genetically diverse breeding populations. Existing approaches often fail to simultaneously capture spatial spectral features, temporal dynamics of crop growth, and the unequal contributions of different growth stages to yield formation, limiting their applicability for breeding-oriented decision making. Here, we developed a hybrid deep learning framework, termed CYPNet, that integrates convolutional neural networks, bidirectional long, short term memory networks, and a multi head self-attention mechanism to enable end-to-end learning and adaptive temporal fusion of multi-temporal unmanned aerial vehicles(UAV)hyperspectral data. Field experiments were conducted using 535 wheat genotypes (262 recombinant inbred line families and 273 natural populations) grown under irrigation and water efficiency conditions in the Huang Huai Hai Plain. Canopy hyperspectral imagery was acquired at four key phenological stages (heading, flowering, early filling, and mid filling). Results showed that multi temporal spectral fusion substantially improved yield prediction accuracy, with CYPNet achieving the highest performance when all stages were integrated (R2 = 0.73, RMSE = 0.75 t/ha, MAE = 0.57 t/ha), outperforming traditional machine learning models, including optimized support vector regression (R2 = 0.62). Model performance exhibited environmental dependence, with slightly higher accuracy under irrigation than under water stress, reflecting increased spectral yield complexity under drought conditions. Importantly, yield predictions from CYPNet were further translated into a breeding-oriented decision framework by integrating drought resistance index, geometric mean productivity, and stress sensitivity index, enabling systematic ranking of drought tolerance across all genotypes. This framework identified 54 highly drought-tolerant wheat lines with stable performance and substantial yield potential, supported by high generalized heritability (H2 = 0.88). Collectively, this study addresses key methodological and application gaps in UAV based yield prediction by linking spatiotemporal hyperspectral modeling with quantitative drought resistance screening, providing a scalable and actionable phenotyping framework to accelerate genetic gain in wheat breeding under water limited environments.
keywords: Drought resistance screening of breeding varieties

title: A spider-inspired superhydrophobic tactile sensor with machine learning-enabled slip detection for damage-free robotic fruit grasping
abstract: The reliable and damage-free robotic harvesting of delicate fruits remains a significant challenge in agricultural automation, primarily due to the lack of tactile sensors that can simultaneously provide high-fidelity force feedback, withstand humid and dusty farm environments, and detect slip events in real time. Herein, we present a bioinspired superhydrophobic tactile sensor engineered for agricultural robotics. Its core is a hollow polydimethylsiloxane/carbon nanotube (PDMS/CNT) microcone array fabricated via a scalable templating process. This architecture synergistically integrates two key mechanisms: a stress-concentration effect from the hollow structure, enabling an ultrahigh sensitivity of 717.39 kPa−1 over a broad range (1–480 kPa), and geometric confinement that stabilizes a solid-air–liquid interface. A facile sieving process deposits a nanostructured hydrophobic silica (SiO2) coating, achieving a contact angle of 158.5° ± 0.6° and a sliding angle of 1°, conferring exceptional self-cleaning and droplet-bouncing capabilities for robust performance in agricultural environments. Crucially, to address the challenge of fruit slip during grasping, we integrated the sensor with a machine learning algorithm. By comparing Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Random Forest models, the Random Forest model was selected, achieving superior slip-detection performance with an accuracy of 0.983, F1-score of 0.983, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.968 on an independent test set. The sensor-integrated adaptive control system successfully enabled real-time pressure monitoring, slip detection, and damage-free grasping of various delicate fruits (oranges, apples, pears, and persimmons). This work provides an effective strategy for developing intelligent, environmentally resilient tactile sensing systems tailored for agricultural robotics and automated fruit handling.

title: A study on vegetation specular reflection removal method based on fusion of Mueller matrix polarization parameters and spectral information
abstract: Specular reflection is a prevalent disturbance factor in both leaf-scale and canopy-scale vegetation remote sensing. It depends on leaf surface properties and does not provide information about internal leaf composition, thereby affecting the inversion of biochemical parameters based on spectral indices. Traditional methods often fail to adequately address this issue, as they struggle to decouple specular reflection from diffuse scattering without compromising vital spectral and structural details. To overcome this critical limitation, this study introduces a novel specular reflection removal method based on the fusion of Mueller matrix polarization parameters and spectral information. A ground-based, time-sequential Mueller matrix multispectral system was constructed to acquire multi-polarization and multi-band data. By analyzing the Mueller matrix’s differential response to specular and diffuse reflection, highlight-sensitive and scatter-robust elements were selected to construct Mueller Matrix Polarization Parameters (MMPs). These were combined with red and near-infrared a priori spectral information to develop the specular reflection removal index—Integrated NDVI-Mueller Vegetation Index (INMVI). This index effectively suppresses surface reflection while preserving spectral detail and textural structure. Leaf-scale experiments validated the method across different health levels and two morphologically distinct plant species (Aucuba japonica var. variegata and the highly glossy Philodendron selloum Koch), as well as under varying illumination intensities from 8 to 125 lx. INMVI achieved high accuracy in estimating relative chlorophyll content (Soil and Plant Analysis Development, SPAD) (R2 = 0.9058, RMSE = 5.6753) and demonstrated exceptional illumination-invariant stability (R2 > 0.87 across all light intensities). Results indicate that the proposed method effectively eliminates specular reflection under diverse geometric, lighting, and surface conditions. Compared to traditional spectral indices, it better preserves leaf texture and detail while improving the SPAD estimation performance. This provides a robust specular reflection removal strategy for precise vegetation health monitoring under complex conditions.

title: Corrigendum to “Concept and rule guided neural network for early crop leaf nutrient deficiency diagnosis” [Comput. Electron. Agric. 248 (2026) 111735]
Advancing site-specific disease and pest management in precision agriculture: From reasoning-driven foundation models to adaptive, feedback-based learning
abstract: Site-specific disease management (SSDM) in agricultural crops has witnessed tremendous advancements over the past few decades using conventional machine and deep learning (ML & DL) approaches for real-time computer vision applications. This research has evolved from handcrafted feature extraction to large-scale automated feature learning in single-modality datasets. However, with the rise of foundation models (FMs), the way large-scale crop disease datasets are processed is being fundamentally transformed. Unlike convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which are inherently single-modality architectures and require post-fusion strategies to integrate heterogenous data streams, vision-language FMs provide unified embedding spaces where visual and textual representations are jointly learned from the same training dataset. This enables richer, more coherent cross-modal reasoning, allowing models to interpret disease symptoms described in text, infer relationships between symptoms and management factors, and support interactive Q&A platforms for growers and extension educators. Beyond visual and textual reasoning, FMs are also serving as backbone architectures for robotic perception and decision-making, bridging the gap between scene understanding and physical action in field environments. In this context, the integration of adaptive, imitation, and reinforcement learning (AL, IL, & RL) in robotics is enabling novel applications for field-based disease management. Therefore, this study reviewed ≈40 research articles to highlight the application of FMs for SSDM in crops, focusing on two primary themes: large-language models (LLMs), and vision language models (VLMs). Additionally, the extended role of FMs in enabling AL, IL, RL, and digital twin (DT) frameworks for robotics-based targeted spraying is also discussed. Based on the results and discussion, several key conclusions emerge from this review: (a) FMs are gaining traction, with a notable increase in reported technical literature during 2023-2024, (b) VLMs are being leveraged more than LLMs, with a five-to-tenfold increase in published articles from 2023 to 2024, (c) RL and AL remain in their infancy for developing smart spraying technologies that learn from experience, (d) integrating DTs with RL in cyber-physical systems offer a transformative approach for simulating targeted spraying in virtual environments, (e) addressing sim-to-real gap, the performance drop when models trained in simulated environments are deployed in real-world disease scenarios, will be critical for robust and scalable management systems, (f) while perception models for disease detection are advancing, human-robot collaboration and human-in-the-loop (HiTL) approaches remain underexplored in field-scale crop disease management systems where robots autonomously detect early symptoms and humans validate uncertain cases, and (g) continued advancements in FMs. Multi-modal integration, and real-time feedback are expected to drive the next generation of SSDM technologies.

title: EnvGreenAE: A denoising-enhanced transformer autoencoder for greenhouse anomaly detection
abstract: Timely and reliable anomaly detection is critical for intelligent greenhouse systems, as abnormal environmental conditions will adversely affect crop growth and yield. However, greenhouse anomaly detection remains particularly challenging, as environmental variables exhibit strong coupling and are simultaneously influenced by biological processes, management operations, and external meteorological conditions, producing complex spatiotemporal dynamics. To address these challenges, two key observations motivate this work. First, greenhouse variables form a coupled system, necessitating full-environment multivariate detection rather than single-variable analysis. Second, reconstruction-based modeling is more appropriate than forecasting for greenhouse monitoring, as it captures normal patterns without predicting complex environmental changes, thus avoiding overfitting to noise and minor fluctuations in the data. Based on these, EnvGreenAE, a self-supervised autoencoder framework with denoising enhancement, is proposed. The model integrates a Transformer encoder for capturing long-range temporal dependencies and inter-variable relationships, a dilated temporal decoder to extract multi-scale features for reconstruction, and a denoising training strategy to improve robustness against noise. The overall architecture is intentionally lightweight, as greenhouse data are typically limited in scale but rich in inter-variable correlations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EnvGreenAE outperforms a range of state-of-the-art baselines across various evaluation metrics, achieving a precision of 0.9410, recall of 0.9738, accuracy of 0.9797, and F1-score of 0.9571. In summary, EnvGreenAE offers a robust solution for anomaly detection in intelligent agriculture, supporting timely responses to microclimate variations and contributing to the stability and efficiency of data-driven greenhouse management.

title: Data-driven optimization of CO2 regulation intervals in controlled environment agriculture
abstract: Precision carbon regulation in controlled environment agriculture (CEA) is essential for promoting crop growth and enhancing energy use efficiency. However, existing CO2 regulation strategies are predominantly based on fixed setpoints or empirically defined intervals, which fail to adequately capture nonlinear crop physiological responses, environmental interactions, and multiobjective trade-offs under practical conditions. To address these issues, this study formulates a data-driven CO2 regulation optimization problem and proposes a hybrid optimization framework. First, a support vector regression-based photosynthetic rate (Pn) model is developed to provide quantitative feedback for regulation design. Second, a biologically-informed constrained non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II is designed to identify feasible CO2 regulation intervals under physiological and operational constraints, improving both convergence efficiency and solution quality. Third, a hybrid decision-making module integrates the best-worst method for weight determination and the measurement of alternatives and ranking according to compromise solution method for solution ranking, enabling robust selection from the Pareto-optimal set. Comprehensive comparative and ablation experiments verify the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Compared with Pn maximum strategies, the proposed method reduced Pn by 17.48% while significantly improving CO2 utilization efficiency (CUE) by 42.16%. It also achieves comparable Pn and CUE with lower CO2 input and fewer device activations than threshold-based strategies. Real-world validation shows reductions of over 40% in CO2 supplementation frequency and 16% in total CO2 dosage. Additional experiments on cucumber and eggplant further demonstrate the transferability of the proposed framework across crop types. Overall, this study provides an extensible solution for sustainable CO2 management in CEA systems.
keywords: Measurement of alternatives and ranking according to compromise Solution (MARCOS)

title: Multi-band microwave sensor for agricultural microsample analysis using dual asymmetric metamaterial resonators toward enhanced and balanced full-band sensitivity
abstract: Rapid, non-destructive dielectric analysis of agricultural micro-samples (e.g., 20 μL of liquid or 0.2 g of powder) is crucial for precision agriculture and food quality control. However, in dielectric-based analysis of mixed micro-samples, situations may arise where different sample compositions exhibit similar dielectric properties at a single frequency. Therefore, effective sensing technology requires multi-frequency detection to mitigate such ambiguities. Owing to the advantages of electromagnetic scaling effects, multi-frequency detection of micro-samples exhibits lower sensitivity in the low-frequency bands than at higher frequencies, yet greater measurement stability than in the high-frequency bands. Thus, enhancing low-frequency sensitivity to achieve balanced sensitivity across multiple frequency bands is both a pathway and a challenge for advancing dielectric detection applications. This study proposed a quad-band microwave resonant sensor that integrates multiple dielectric interference modes to achieve highly sensitive detection of agricultural micro-samples. The sensor comprises two metamaterial resonators with identical topologies but different geometric parameters. Using field perturbation theory and frequency convergence effects, we analyzed the behavior of three key interference modes (Modes I, II, and III). The theoretical model was validated through simulation and experiments, and the performance of each mode in terms of sensitivity and effective detection range was compared. The results show that Modes I and II exhibit substantially higher sensitivity in the low-frequency band than Mode III. This study proposed a strategy for enhancing low-frequency sensitivity in multi-frequency sensors and provided new insights into balanced band-sensing technology. The approach demonstrates promising potential for application in micro-sample dielectric analysis, with potential uses in monitoring the quality of liquid agricultural products, detecting nutrient concentrations in fertilizers, and assessing seed viability.

title: Development and validation of an interpretable EEG-based deep learning framework for estrus detection in dairy cows
abstract: Electroencephalographic (EEG) signals exhibit stable and reproducible differences between estrus and non-estrus dairy cows, indicating that central nervous system activity reflects estrus-related regulation beyond external behavioral expression. Analysis across multiple EEG domains shows that estrus-associated neural modulation involves coordinated changes across frequency bands and recording channels and remains identifiable under varying behavioral conditions. Using multi-channel EEG recordings collected from 90 dairy cows, estrus detection was evaluated in a cross-subject evaluation, in which training and testing were conducted on data from different individuals. Under this evaluation protocol, the EEG-based approach achieved an accuracy of 92.7 ± 1.5%, an area under the curve of 94.0 ± 1.4%, a sensitivity of 94.1 ± 1.4%, and a specificity of 95.4 ± 1.3%, demonstrating robust discrimination across individuals rather than reliance on individual-specific neural patterns. Comparative model evaluation under unified experimental conditions indicates that appropriate feature representation and modeling strategies consistently capture estrus-related neural patterns. Attention-based interpretability analysis further reveals that EEG frequency bands contribute unequally to estrus discrimination, with low-frequency components, particularly the delta band, exhibiting the highest and most stable contribution across behavioral conditions. These results support EEG as a physiologically meaningful and interpretable information source for cross-individual estrus detection in dairy cows.

title: MOSP: A Multi-Orientation Sequential Picking Planning for Robotic Harvest of Breeding Cotton
abstract: Frequent rainfall and strong winds necessitate timely and phased cotton harvesting, thereby driving advances in robotic harvesting. However, the irregular orientation and dense distribution of cotton bolls pose a major challenge to achieving efficient harvesting with a low missed-pick rate. To address this challenge, a multi-orientation sequential picking planning method is proposed, integrating an on-the-move picking strategy and a multi-surface picking end-effector capable of harvesting cotton bolls from multiple orientations. First, the OrientCot-YOLO model is proposed for the orientation identification and localization of cotton bolls with high inference speed to form a robust foundation for next multi-surface picking plan. Then, a directional hybrid weighting method is proposed to optimize on-the-move picking sequence planning, which integrates directional and three-dimensional distance weighting for target prioritization, and identifies the optimal picking surface through normal vector matching with cosine similarity. Finally, an optimal picking path planning method based on multi-surface picking end-effector is developed. The method integrates multi-objective optimization and speed dynamic compensation to calculate the end-effector pre-picking point, and employs RRT-Connect with NURBS smoothing to generate the optimal picking path. In the gazebo simulation experiment (506 cotton bolls), compared with the Random Traversal and Euclidean Distance methods, the MOSP method improved the picking efficiency by 34.9% and 15.8%, respectively, while reducing the omission rate by 22.34% and 13.85%. In field trials (200 bolls), the omission rate was 13.7% and the picking efficiency was 6.9 s/boll, including efficiency losses caused by failed picks due to branch movement. This method improves picking efficiency and reduces the omission rate of cotton picking, providing an effective solution for on-the-move picking in complex and dense environments.

title: SMART: Structured multimodal agricultural retrieval-augmented transformer for plant disease diagnosis
abstract: Real-world plant disease diagnosis requires robustness to long-tailed class distributions and variable input quality, yet prevailing multimodal approaches do not explicitly address these challenges. This study presents SMART, a framework that integrates structured linguistic guidance with retrieval-augmented inference. Evaluation of 37,586 images across 48 disease categories yields three findings. First, structured captions outperform LLM-generated narratives, with the vision-only baseline exceeding all LLM approaches on the 20-class pilot, demonstrating that semantic precision, not descriptive complexity, drives effective vision-language alignment. Second, we distinguish between training-time and inference-time challenges: long-tailed degradation is mitigated through asymmetric loss design, while input quality variability is addressed through a dual-pathway mechanism in which semantic anchoring constrains predictions under related errors, and the retrieval-based safety net ensures bounded degradation under noisy inputs. Third, frequency-stratified analysis reveals a division of labor: semantic anchoring benefits high-frequency classes, while the retrieval-based safety net preferentially compensates rare classes. These complementary mechanisms support a human-in-the-loop workflow that transforms single-pass diagnosis into collaborative verification. SMART achieves F1 = 0.9767, surpassing fine-tuned CNNs (best F1 = 0.9118) and 22 multimodal foundation models (best F1 = 0.8904). The primary contributions of this work are: (i) a systematic benchmark of caption form-structured versus LLM-generated as an experimental variable in agricultural vision-language alignment; (ii) a factorial decomposition that quantitatively isolates the independent and complementary roles of semantic anchoring and retrieval-based compensation across frequency strata; and (iii) a statistically validated, human-in-the-loop diagnostic framework applicable to large-scale, imbalanced disease taxonomies.

title: Research on LED supplementary lighting decision-making framework for greenhouse tomatoes based on yield-oriented
abstract: Efficient regulation of supplementary lighting in greenhouse tomato production remains a challenge owing to the lack of quantitative decision-making methods and the strong coupling among environmental factors. To address this issue, this study proposes a yield-oriented LED supplementary lighting decision framework for greenhouse tomato production, which directly links the target yield to dynamic lighting regulation under natural light variability. Within this framework, the required annual light integral (ALI) corresponding to a target yield is first determined from the yield–light response relationship via data-driven estimation and marginal effect analysis. This ALI is then allocated to the daily light integral (DLI) at the tomato growth week scale based on dynamic light allocation (Dx), which simultaneously accounts for the stage-specific characteristics of tomato growth (Wy,x) and the phenological variations in natural light availability (Px). In the validation experiment, a target yield of 22 kg·m⁻2·year⁻1 for cherry tomatoes was set according to actual production. The framework determined the required ALI of 6.92 kmol·m⁻2·year⁻1 (toplighting) and 3.74 kmol·m⁻2·year⁻1 (interlighting), which was then allocated to the weekly DLI ranging from 0 to 32 mol·m⁻2·day⁻1 throughout the growing period. The results demonstrated that compared with the empirically derived supplementary lighting strategy, the strategy based on the proposed decision-making framework increased the yield target achievement rate of cherry tomatoes by 17.3%, enhanced light use efficiency (LUE) by 28.6%, and improved electrical energy use efficiency (EUE) by 40.7%. In addition, the framework incorporates uncertainty handling through error propagation and sensitivity analysis, ensuring stable decision performance under varying environmental conditions. Overall, this study provides a practical and robust decision-support approach for yield-oriented and energy-efficient supplementary lighting regulation in greenhouse production systems.

title: Vineyard Yield Prediction using Radar Images and a Convolutional Neural Network
abstract: Predicting vineyard yield before harvest is valuable for optimizing logistics, resource allocation, and grape quality management. Traditional yield estimation methods based on manual sampling or optical imaging often suffer from high uncertainty due to occlusions, illumination variability, and grape bunch concealment. In this paper, we propose a deep learning–based approach for vineyard yield prediction using proximal millimeter-wave radar images, which are inherently robust to lighting conditions and capable of detecting partially or fully hidden grapes. A convolutional neural network (CNN) is used to learn the relevant feature representation directly from radar images acquired between consecutive vineyard posts and to estimate grape weight through end-to-end regression. However, radar images are affected by clutter, i.e., unwanted echoes that degrade prediction accuracy, particularly in low-yield scenarios. To address this issue, we introduce a novel graphical deep learning method (G_DL) based on image pair averaging, which reduces the influence of clutter during training and inference. The proposed method was validated using radar datasets collected over four growing seasons (2019–2022). The baseline CNN model achieved validation errors of approximately 15–18% (R2 ≈ 0.64), while the proposed G_DL method reduced the prediction error to approximately 8%. The results demonstrate that combining radar imaging with the proposed graphical deep learning strategy significantly improves yield prediction accuracy and robustness under the studied vineyard conditions, where multiple grape varieties coexist without requiring variety-specific calibration. This approach shows strong potential for integration into precision viticulture systems to support pre-harvest operational decisions related to logistics, workforce planning, and yield management.

title: Design and evaluation of two heuristic-based interactive controllers for selective apple harvest
abstract: The picking action used by an apple harvesting robot has a critical impact on post-harvest fruit quality and long-term tree health. A poorly executed pick can lead to excessive fruit bruising, stem pulls, and limb breaks. The prior work has typically considered the picking phase an open loop motion control problem, using patterns such as linear pull, inclined pull, pull-twist, etc. In this paper, we consider picking an interaction control problem whereby force feedback is used to guide robot motion. We designed two picking controllers that utilize different strategies to detach the apple. The first controller keeps a constant tension in the stem while moving perpendicularly to the measured force in order to replicate a pendulum-like motion. The second uses a simplex search to seek out the stiffest direction, attempting to minimize plant damage by minimizing plant deflection. To evaluate performance, we conducted picking trials on a modular orchard testbed and performed a logistic regression to evaluate the effect of controller and plant properties on the rate of spur break events. We found that plant and fruit growth angles strongly influenced the observed rate of spur breaks. Compared to a benchmark controller, the stiffness seeking controller reduced the rate of spur breaks from an overall rate of 44.7% to 12.1%. The stiffness seeking controller also had the fastest separation rate with an average picking time of 1.00 s, compared to 2.34 s for the constant tension controller. During outdoor field experiments, preliminary results showed that controller performance in a commercial apple orchard was similar to what was observed in the lab on a physical proxy.

title: Design and evaluation of a small arched shed construction machine
abstract: The traditional manual construction of small arched shed is characterized by high labor intensity, low efficiency, and uneven quality, which restricts its large-scale application. A multi-functional mechanism that integrates shed pole installation, film laying, and covering was designed to enhance small arched shed processes. This enhancement included a kinematic model of the pole insertion mechanism, the coordinated motion patterns of the mechanical arm and the pressing arm. This aimed to improve—grasping and bending, pole insertion, and precise control over the motion trajectory of the shed pole. The designed and constructed machine featured multiple adjustable components capable of. Independently or jointly adjusting the inclination angle, spacing, width, height, and insertion depth of the shed poles. This was achieved by adjusting the initial phase of the transmission sprocket, gear transmission ratio, horizontal spacing of the manipulator arms, and the extension length of the bending bracket, potentially improving the agronomic requirements for four-row cotton planting. Field tests showed that the machine operated stably. The pole insertion depth, thickness and width of the soil cover on the film edges, shed spacing, width, and height had qualification rates of 100%, whereas the pole perpendicularity achieved a qualification rate of 96.5%. All indicators exceeded industry standards. The test results verify the reliability, adaptability, and operational accuracy of the newly designed mechanism for small arched sheds for cotton. This study provides theoretical and equipment solutions for the mechanized construction of small arched sheds, significant for the cotton production.

title: Active far-to-close perception via optimal fishbone-view estimation for robotic truss tomato harvesting
abstract: Efficient robotic harvesting of truss tomatoes demands precise perception of fruit morphology within clusters to ensure collision-free manipulation. To address this challenge, a unified framework integrating far-range dual-modal object detection with close-range camera pose estimation is presented to acquire an optimal fishbone view. This canonical orientation for truss tomatoes aligns the cluster plane with the camera image plane, thereby revealing the symmetrical distribution of fruits and clarifying the topological structure of peduncle-fruit connections to facilitate accurate manipulation. First, a lightweight network termed TOLONet is proposed to mitigate interference from complex backgrounds and occlusions. This architecture employs a depth-prior-guided RGB feature fusion strategy alongside multi-scale attention mechanisms for robust feature extraction. Second, to recover fine-grained depth details often lost in far-range imaging, a depth texture enhancement strategy based on DepthAnything-AC is implemented, combined with RobustSAM to generate high-fidelity point clouds of truss tomatoes. Third, by leveraging the orthogonal projection of the enhanced point clouds, the close-range camera pose is derived in closed form, directly enabling motion planning to achieve the optimal fishbone view. Experimental results demonstrate that TOLONet achieves an mAP@0.5:0.95 of 83.1% with an inference speed of 6.5 ms, outperforming state-of-the-art YOLO and DETR-based models. Furthermore, the proposed fishbone-view estimation method achieves a success rate exceeding 80% across frontal and tilted orientations, effectively bridging the perception-to-action gap for autonomous harvesting systems.

title: An intelligent data-driven framework for optimizing wheat management toward high yields with reduced nitrogen inputs
abstract: Achieving a balance between high and stable wheat yields and reduced nitrogen inputs remains a major challenge for sustainable agriculture. To address the limited generalizability of current nitrogen management models across environment and management gradients, this study develops an AI- and data-driven decision framework for wheat based on a harmonized global field trial database. The framework is built on datasets compiled from published field experiments and integrates two modeling solutions (AutoGluon and TabPFN) to predict and optimize wheat yield and nitrogen uptake across different climate zones. The models exhibit strong performance and robustness, with an R 2 of 0.88 and an RMSE of 26.3 kg N·ha⁻ 1 for predicted nitrogen uptake and an R 2 of 0.82 and an RMSE of 865.9 kg DM·ha⁻ 1 for predicted yield. Scenario analysis shows that nitrogen application can be reduced by 13% while maintaining yield, and that improved management can increase average yield by 19.6% while reducing nitrogen application by 18.2%, demonstrating the potential for multi-factor synergistic optimization. Analysis of management contributions using sensitivity analysis and Shapley decomposition revealed that improvements in nitrogen application methods and forms, as well as multiple applications, had the greatest impact on yield enhancement. Shapley decomposition further validated these conclusions and quantified the relative contributions of each management factor under multi-factor conditions. Overall, this study provides quantitative evidence that AI-driven management can identify agronomic interventions that increase yields while reducing nitrogen inputs, thereby informing scalable, environment-specific decision frameworks for wheat production.

title: 3D reconstruction and segmentation of grape bunches for robotic berry thinning
abstract: Table grape thinning requires selective removal of 20–40% of berries from dense clusters. In practice, workers decide which berries to remove by considering both the approximate berry count and local 3D spatial characteristics such as crowding and relative positioning. Automating this task is challenging because conventional 2D image-based approaches suffer from occlusion-related counting errors and lack explicit 3D spatial information necessary for reliable manipulation.We propose a novel vision-based method that reconstructs the three-dimensional structure of grape clusters from multi-view camera images. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) is used to learn a volumetric scene representation, from which a dense, low-noise point cloud is extracted via depth back-projection, and RANSAC-based geometric fitting models individual berries and stems, enabling berry-level segmentation and orientation estimation for manipulation planning. The perception pipeline is integrated with an eye-in-hand camera on a Fanuc CRX-5iA collaborative robot, allowing direct transformation of detected berry positions into robot coordinates for accurate approach to the target berries.Experiments on 52 grape bunches demonstrates that RANSAC-based geometric fitting outperforms that learning-based SoftGroup++ method for 3D berry instance segmentation (92.1% vs 82.8% average precision) while requiring no annotated training data. Berry counting error is reduced by 52% compared with a state-of-the-art 2D method (MAE: 1.1 vs 2.3 berries). In 35 physical manipulation trials, the system achieved an 85.7% pre-grasp reachability rate and an 83.3% conditional target success rate; including collision-free grip, the end-to-end success rate was 96% with stem-aligned orientation versus 78.26% without, demonstrating the manipulation benefit of structure-aware pose estimation, providing the first end-to-end validation from neural reconstruction to robotic manipulation for grape berry thinning.

title: FEAFace: Feature enhancing and adaptive feature space reconstruction for large pose livestock face recognition
abstract: Robust individual recognition is fundamental to enabling precision livestock farming, underpinning critical applications from individualized health monitoring to optimized feeding regimes. As a dominant computer vision solution for this task, face recognition has seen significant success in humans, yet its extension to animals faces unique challenges in farm environments — most critically, the extreme scarcity of frontal face images. To address this core limitation, we propose FEAFace — a novel recognition model leveraging adaptive feature space reconstruction. By mapping features from multiple poses into a unified space and optimizing feature distribution, our model significantly improves recognition under large-pose conditions. Furthermore, we introduce a detachable auxiliary task integrated with an enhanced hyperspherical manifold loss, boosting accuracy without computational overhead. Extensive experiments are conducted on two newly established public benchmarks, CattleFace-MP and DeerFace-MP, which are collected from real-world cattle and deer farms and specifically designed for large-pose livestock face recognition. The datasets contain multi-view images with substantial pose, illumination, and appearance variations, addressing the practical scarcity of frontal animal face images. Built upon a ResNet-derived backbone, FEAFace achieves Rank-1 accuracies of 98.043% on Simmental cattle, 90.465% on Working cattle, and 90.014% on deer recognition benchmarks, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by margins of 1.996%, 3.089%, and 1.932%, respectively. These results demonstrate the robustness and adaptability of the proposed method under challenging pose variations, highlighting its effectiveness for practical livestock individual identification in intelligent management systems such as automated feeding, health monitoring, and behavior analysis. Our datasets and code is available at https://github.com/B532Orange.

title: S2G-Net: an asymmetric cross-modal network for tiny cotton terminal-bud detection and sparse depth completion in real fields
abstract: Accurate perception of cotton terminal buds for automated topping remains challenging because extremely small targets and dense canopy occlusions hinder conventional RGB-based detectors, while field depth measurements are often sparse and noisy. To address these limitations, this study formulates cotton terminal-bud perception as a joint problem of tiny terminal-bud detection and sparse depth completion, and proposes S2G-Net (Semantics-to-Geometry Network), an asymmetric cross-modal RGB-D framework for this task. S2G-Net adopts a dual-branch architecture with an RGB detection branch and a sparse-depth completion branch, which are connected by a Cross-Modal Guidance (CMG) module that transfers high-level semantic priors from RGB features to the depth pathway through channel-wise and spatial-wise modulation. This semantics-to-geometry design improves depth completion under severe sparsity while preserving the stability of the RGB detection branch through uncertainty-weighted multi-task learning. Experiments on a real-world cotton terminal-bud RGB-D dataset show that S2G-Net achieves an F1-score of 72.56% and an mAP50-95 of 35.23%, corresponding to relative improvements of 4.0% and 5.9% over the best RGB-only YOLO baseline, respectively. For depth completion with only 5% valid depth pixels, S2G-Net achieves a mean absolute error of 0.0023 m, representing a 25.8% reduction compared with the best single-task baseline. These results show that the proposed asymmetric semantics-guided framework improves both semantic detection and depth completion under severe field sparsity, providing a stronger perception basis for automated cotton topping in real field environments.

title: ECroPS: An advanced crop modelling platform with an enhanced WOFOST for multilayer soil water and nitrogen dynamics
abstract: Robust climate change risk assessments require crop models that better represent the impacts of climate extremes as well as water and nutrient dynamics. To better quantify the uncertainties, they also need models that can be easily run to simulate large ensembles. To address these needs, a novel crop modelling platform, ECroPS (Engine for Crop Parallelizable Simulations), is here proposed. It builds on an improved WOFOST model having a multilayer soil model with soil nitrogen component to enhance the representation of water and nutrient dynamics. ECroPS is here tested at field scale (in Italy, Germany, and the Netherlands), with cultivar calibration based on detailed field measurements on maize and wheat. To explore and characterise the behaviour of ECroPS, simulations are also performed under future climate conditions, assuming no changes in agro-management, at two of the experimental sites. The main results point to the overall good performance of the model, particularly under water stress, that better represents crop responses and simulates nitrogen content. Thanks to its implementation and its flexibility, ECroPS offers a scalable and modular approach that can be used to run large ensemble as well as test sensitivities and responses to specific parametrisation, such as the one on atmospheric CO 2 concentration. ECroPS is open-source and freely available.

title: Improved causal attention mechanism and semi-supervised learning integrated deep learning model for blueberry ripeness detection
abstract: The high nutritional value of blueberry has driven production scale expansion, with efficient harvesting and precision management becoming key for industrial upgrading—blueberry ripeness grading is its core link. Mainstream fruit ripeness detection methods use ordinary or hyperspectral images as data foundations, relying on machine learning-based computer vision. However, they have two critical limitations: only focusing on data correlation while overlooking causality, failing to unearth the intrinsic links between fruit growth and ripeness and thus resulting in misjudgments in complex scenarios; and poor cost and deployment adaptability, relying on large-scale manual annotations and high equipment costs, which cannot meet low-cost portable field needs. To address these, this study takes YOLO11 as the baseline and proposes YOLO11-WBO, a semi-supervised lightweight model for blueberry ripeness grading. Structurally, it integrates three customized modules: C2PSA_BCA includes causal attention and blueberry-specific features to enhance key information representation; C3k2_WT adopts wavelet convolution for accurate multi-scale feature extraction; C3k2_OREPA uses “multi-branch optimization during training and single convolution deployment during inference” to improve feature efficiency. A semi-supervised learning framework reduces reliance on large annotated data. Experiments on a blueberry dataset show YOLO11-WBO outperforms the original YOLO11n by 3.3 % in Precision and 4.6 % in mAP@50:95, maintains 8.33 ms per-image inference speed, and cuts annotation effort by 63 %. This work provides a low-annotation, low-cost, high-robustness solution for blueberry ripeness grading, with significant practical value and broad promotion prospects.

title: RT-BFE network: A lightweight deep learning model for real-time beef freshness evaluation and edge devices deployment
abstract: Real-time and non-destructive assessment of beef freshness is crucial for food safety, quality control, and waste reduction. However, routine evaluation still relies on destructive laboratory measurements or computationally heavy vision models that are difficult to deploy on consumer-level devices. Here, we develop a lightweight real-time beef freshness evaluation (RT-BFE) network that links image features to spoilage-related regions and is suitable for deployment on edge devices. First, total volatile basic nitrogen (TVB-N) and total viable counts (TVC) were measured in beef samples (420 pieces stored for 0–6 days) to define three freshness levels (fresh, accepted, and deteriorated). Second, beef images in RGB, HSV, and L*a*b* color spaces were compared to find the optimal color space for beef freshness evaluation. Third, three modules, namely efficient bottleneck (E-bneck), cascade atrous spatial pyramid pooling (CASPP), and convolutional block attention module (CBAM), were designed in the RT-BFE network to strengthen its recognition ability and reduce computational cost. Finally, the model was quantized and deployed on edge devices for practical applications. Experimental results show that the L*a*b* provides the most discriminative representation for beef freshness classification. Comparative experiments against ten image classification CNNs demonstrate that the RT-BFE model achieves a favorable trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, attaining the Accuracy and F1 of 95.238% and 95.238% with only 1.106 M Parameters and 59.347 M FLOPs, and reaching 72.301 frames per second. Subsequently, the proposed RT-BFE model is successfully deployed on edge devices in FP16-quantized form for practical applications. The deployments on a smartphone and a Jetson Orin Nano platform achieve average inference times of 32 ms and 14 ms, respectively, while maintaining an accuracy of 93.33% on both devices, demonstrating real-time inference capability and confirming its potential for in-situ beef freshness monitoring in practical agri-food scenarios.

title: MSFA: A method for reference-free usability scoring via structural fidelity of field acquired maize leaf images
abstract: Field maize scouting operates in unstructured conditions where blur and mixed-focus degradations frequently compromise leaf ROI usability and cause overconfident downstream failures. In this study, the Maize Structural Fidelity Assessor (MSFA), a reference-free usability scoring module, was proposed for the estimation of maize-structure fidelity and usability risk by fusing learned features with maize-guided structural cues, including venation anisotropy, gradient-based sharpness consistency, and texture-entropy statistics. A naturally captured Challenge Field Subset (CFS) was constructed for the stress-test in long-tail field degradations. Results presented that MSFA substantially improved robustness on CFS, outperforming generic CNN baselines (72.1%). The quality-state recognition accuracy achieved 92.37%, while the high-confidence errors under localized or compound blur reduced. Deployed on scouting video streams, MSFA-based screening identified that only about one third of frames were usable for further image processing. These findings suggest the feasibility of quality-aware frame selection within short temporal windows. Real-time performance was achieved on a Jetson Xavier NX using TensorRT FP16, suggesting the feasibility of real-time quality screening and risk-aware reporting for in-field scouting under the tested deployment setting.

title: A deep learning-based adaptive control system for intelligent drying of horticultural flowers: A novel approach to reducing postharvest losses
abstract: Significant postharvest losses during the drying of horticultural flowers pose a threat to the stability and economic viability of their industrial supply chains. Existing drying processes, which rely on static, fixed-parameter settings, fail to effectively balance drying efficiency with final product quality, thereby exacerbating this challenge. This study developed and validated a deep learning-based adaptive control system for hot-air drying using chrysanthemums as a representative model, which enables dynamic regulation of drying parameters based on real-time monitoring of appearance quality. For the accurate online assessment of appearance quality, this proposed system incorporated a Spatial Interaction-Aware Segmentation (SIA-S) network. Trained on a dataset of 6889 images (partitioned into a 7:2:1 ratio for training, validation, and testing), the network achieved an mIoU of 96.20% and a Precision of 97.85%. These quantified appearance quality indicators were then fused with sensor-derived drying rates to train a Temporal Feature-Enhanced LSTM (TFE-LSTM), which outperformed standard baseline models (CNN, LSTM, and CNN-LSTM) in predicting quality evolution trajectories (R2 > 0.9970). Based on real-time predictions, the adaptive control system dynamically regulated drying parameters at 30-min intervals, yielding an optimized 300-min drying process. The resulting optimal trajectory consisted of a temperature sequence of [40, 60, 60, 60, 60, 60, 50, 60, 50, 60] oC and an air velocity sequence of [1.2, 2.8, 2.8, 2.8, 2.8, 2.8, 2.0, 2.8, 2.0, 2.8] m/s. Experimental results showed that compared to fixed-parameter drying, the proposed strategy significantly (p < 0.05) reduced drying time, achieved energy savings of up to 36.73%, improved the color profile (higher lightness and lower yellow index), inhibited shrinkage (a minimum shrinkage ratio of 0.51), and increased retention of marker phenolic compounds. A comprehensive evaluation score of 0.65 further validated the system’s effectiveness. Overall, this adaptive control system provides a theoretical and technical foundation for the intelligent drying of horticultural flowers.

title: Design and evaluation of an active shielded capacitive sensor system for real-time wheat seed mass-flow monitoring
abstract: Capacitive sensors have been widely used in seeding monitoring systems. However, the monitoring accuracy of capacitive wheat seed mass flow sensors is often degraded by environmental temperature–humidity variations and stray capacitance effects. To address these issues, this study developed an active-shielding wheat mass flow sensor (AS-WMFS) together with a corresponding monitoring algorithm. By introducing active shielding electrodes, the effective sensing regions of the monitoring and environmental compensation capacitors were confined to the intended sensing space. An environment-compensated dynamic capacitive integration algorithm (EC-DCIA) was further proposed to enable real-time monitoring under both constant and variable seed mass flow conditions. Bench tests were conducted to compare the environmental compensation capability, shielding performance, and monitoring accuracy of the AS-WMFS with those of a non-shielded wheat mass flow sensor (NS-WMFS). The results show that, compared with the NS-WMFS, the AS-WMFS reduced the influence of environmental variations on the baseline capacitance by 77% and significantly improved the stability of the sensing region. The average monitoring accuracies of the AS-WMFS reached 99.46% under constant mass flow and 99.19% under variable mass flow conditions, exceeding those of the NS-WMFS (98.93% and 98.78%, respectively), with particularly pronounced advantages at high seed mass flow rates. This study provides a useful basis for the design of high-accuracy, interference-resistant capacitive systems for wheat seed mass-flow monitoring.

title: Data fusion of Vis-NIR and pXRF with machine learning for predicting andic properties in volcanic soils
abstract: Volcanic soils exhibit distinctive andic properties, including organic carbon (OC), bulk density (Bd), phosphate retention (Pret), and the sum of ammonium oxalate-extractable aluminum and half iron (Alo + 0.5Feo), and play an important role in agricultural production and ecological functions. However, conventional determination of andic properties relies on destructive, labor-intensive, and time-consuming wet chemistry analyses. Soil spectroscopic techniques such as visible and near-infrared (Vis-NIR) spectroscopy and portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) provide rapid and non-destructive alternatives. This study aimed to elucidate the relationships between andic properties and signals from Vis-NIR and pXRF, and to evaluate the accuracy of sensor-based models for predicting andic properties and soil classification. A total of 93 soil samples were collected from 24 pedons of volcanic soils (0–60 cm depth) in northern Taiwan, including Andisols and Inceptisols. Predictive models were developed using individual sensors and a data fusion approach calibrated with partial least squares regression (PLSR) and the Cubist algorithm. Both Vis-NIR and pXRF signals demonstrated associations with andic properties, while data fusion of these two sensors markedly improved model performance. In particular, the Vis-NIR + pXRF-based model calibrated with Cubist yielded good predictive performance, achieving R2 and LCCC values exceeding 0.90 for OC, Pret, and Alo + 0.5Feo, and R2 = 0.83 and LCCC = 0.89 for Bd. Moreover, 23 out of the 24 studied pedons were correctly classified. Integrating Vis-NIR and pXRF provided an efficient approach for assessing andic properties, improving management and resource-use efficiency in volcanic soils, and supporting sustainable smart agriculture.

title: An interpretable framework using foundation models for fish sex identification
abstract: Accurate sex identification in fish is vital for optimizing breeding and management strategies in aquaculture, particularly for species at the risk of extinction. However, most existing methods are invasive or stressful and may cause additional mortality, posing severe risks to threatened or endangered fish populations. To address these challenges, we propose FishProtoNet, a robust, non-invasive computer vision–based framework for sex identification of delta smelt ( Hypomesus transpacificus ), an endangered fish species native to California, across its full life cycle. Unlike the traditional deep learning methods, FishProtoNet provides interpretability through learned prototype representations while improving robustness by leveraging foundation models to reduce the influence of background noise. Specifically, the FishProtoNet framework consists of three key components: fish regions of interest (ROIs) extraction using visual foundation model, feature extraction from fish ROIs and fish sex identification based on an interpretable prototype network. FishProtoNet demonstrates strong performance in delta smelt sex identification during early spawning and post-spawning stages, achieving the accuracies of 74.40% and 81.16% and corresponding F1 scores of 74.27% and 79.43% respectively. In contrast, delta smelt sex identification at the subadult stage remains challenging for current computer vision methods, likely due to less pronounced morphological differences in immature fish. The source code of FishProtoNet is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhengmiao1/fish_gender_recognition.git .

title: A multi-attention guided convolutional network for real-time unstructured road segmentation and autonomous navigation in greenhouse environments
abstract: Semantic segmentation of unstructured greenhouse roads presents numerous challenges, including high model complexity, limited scene-specific data, and practical deployment constraints. To address the issue of model complexity, a multi-attention guided convolutional network for segmentation (MAGCN-Seg) is proposed. The architecture incorporates a dual-path heterogeneous convolution module to improve directional structural modeling and global contextual perception, and a multi-scale convolutional attention module (MSCAM) to enhance multi-scale semantic representation while suppressing background interference. To mitigate the scarcity of greenhouse-specific data, a monocular-vision-based greenhouse unstructured road dataset (GURD) was designed, and a random cropping-patching (RCP) data augmentation strategy was used to enhance model generalization. Experimental results using the GURD, off-road freespace detection (ORFD), and cavs traversability (CaT) mixed datasets indicated that MAGCN-Seg outperformed state-of-the-art methods, with improvements of 1.3%, 1.4%, and 1.9% in mean intersection over union (mIoU) and 1.1%, 1.7%, and 5.3% in mean pixel accuracy (MPA), respectively. These results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach in complex unstructured road scenarios. To validate its practical applicability, an end-to-end vision-control closed-loop system was developed and deployed in 0.7-m wide greenhouse corridors. The system exhibited real-time inference at 27 frames per second (FPS) on the Jetson AGX Orin platform and maintained stable navigation with a crop clearance distance of 0.02 m. The lateral deviation was controlled at <0.01 m, and the heading error remained below 0.25°, effectively compensating for the limited operational radius of inspection manipulators and demonstrating strong engineering feasibility and robustness.

title: Accurate counting of small and dense Chinese cherry in natural orchard via fruit-oriented perception and sharpening network
abstract: Accurate counting of small dense Chinese cherry (prunus pseudocerasus) is crucial for yield estimation and resource management but remains challenging due to background interference, morphological variation, and fruit adhesion ambiguity. A Fruit-Oriented Perception and Sharpening Network (FOPSN) is proposed to address the challenges by fruit concentration-adaptation and distribution sharpening. Specifically, Progressive Spatial Aggregation Encoder (PSAE) concentrates fruit to reduce background interference through region-aware refinement, and Adaptive Similarity Module (ASM) leverages morphology guided adaptation to achieve cherry recognition of diverse phenotypes. Meanwhile, Interleaved Channel Reconstruction Decoder (ICRD) resolves fruit adhesion ambiguity through dual channel rearrangement to sharpen fruit boundaries. FOPSN achieves a mean absolute error of 2.097, a root mean squared error of 2.838 and frames per second of 73, outperforming existing object detection and density map methods. Moreover, feature map confirms PSAE effectively highlights cherry regions against complex backgrounds, and density map visualization demonstrates the robust adaptation of ASM to diverse fruit morphologies and powerful boundary sharpening capability of ICRD. The proposed method provides a robust and reliable solution to count small and dense Chinese cherries under challenging orchard conditions, including complex backgrounds, morphological variations, and fruit adhesion ambiguity, and this approach can be integrated into practical orchard workflows to provide yield estimation, cultivation regulation, and harvest scheduling in field environments.

title: Tomato harvesting pose estimation based on fruit-stem spatial relationship
abstract: Greenhouse environments are complex and variable, and the diverse postures of fruits pose significant challenges for the automation of harvesting robots. Automated harvesting depends critically on the spatial localization of harvesting points and the estimation of harvesting posture. Pose estimation plays a crucial role in path planning and improving harvesting success rates. This study proposes a harvesting pose estimation method based on the spatial relationship between tomatoes and their main stems. Based on this method, the study designs an apparatus for acquiring ground-truth posture as well as a path-planning scheme. Specifically, the tomato and stem were segmented using a YOLOv8-seg model. A total of 1,125 tomato images was used for training and validation of the segmentation model. The tomato centroid and stem axis served as feature points, and the vector between them represented the harvesting posture. On this basis, the end-effector’s harvesting strategy was planned, and an experimental device was developed for obtaining ground-truth posture data. Segmentation experiments conducted on tomatoes at various relative positions, postures, and viewing angles demonstrated robust segmentation performance, achieving mAP@50 values of 92.9% for tomato fruits and 78.5% for main stems. In greenhouse trials involving pose estimation and robotic validation, the proposed method yields an average 3D grasping orientation error of 16.85°, with a standard deviation of 19.05°. The pose estimation experiments were evaluated on 18 independent tomato samples. These results demonstrate that the method effectively supports automated tomato harvesting and lays the groundwork for future research on intelligent path planning in complex greenhouse scenarios.

title: Hail damage assessment in tomato crops using UAV-based vegetation indices and machine learning-based regression
abstract: Hailstorms are extreme weather events that severely damage plants and reduce crop yields. Traditional hail simulations often use leaf defoliation to assess plant damage, but hail damage is typically classified into several categories. In this study, we simulated eight hail scenarios on tomato plants using water-absorbed and frozen pumice stones of various sizes and quantities to replicate real hail. These simulations were conducted at four developmental stages of the tomato plant. We calculated 62 vegetation indices before and after each simulation. The percentage of hail damage was then estimated using six machine learning regression models and five feature selection methods, including correlation, ReliefF, LASSO, Random Forest Feature Importance (RFFI), and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE). The combination of RFE and the Random Forest model provided the most accurate estimates, with a Pearson correlation coefficient (R) of 0.9019, a mean absolute error (MAE) of 4.7287, and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 5.6991.

title: Open Datasets and AI/GenAI-Driven Computer Vision for Precision Livestock Farming: A Bidirectional Review
abstract: The advancement of Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) depends on high-quality data, yet a systematic understanding of the open data landscape remains fragmented. This review adopts a bidirectional perspective, evaluating both open datasets and the researchers who cited them, with a focus on research objectives and practical applications. Through bidirectional searches of Scopus/Web of Science and digital repositories, 315 open datasets were identified between 2010 and 2025, spanning dairy cows, beef cattle, pigs, poultry, and other species. The majority were released within the last five years, signalling a remarkable data explosion. Peer-reviewed literature remains the primary dissemination engine 63% (n=199), while standalone repositories contribute 37% (n=116), reflecting a shift toward data-first scientific contributions. Species distribution is skewed toward cattle (n=131), followed by swine (n=59) and poultry (n=43). Non-AI computer vision relies on deterministic algorithms exploiting the physical and spectral properties of animal images. Among AI approaches, object detection dominates livestock monitoring, with YOLO architectures and Region-based Convolutional Neural Networks leading the field. Generative AI — particularly Foundation Models (FM) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANS) — has mitigated the scarcity of labelled data, superseding manual annotation through automated frameworks such as the Accelerated Data Engine. These resources are evolving into the backbone of Large Language Models (LLMs) and visual-language frameworks, enabling herd reasoning and predictive diagnostics, marking the transition from reactive to proactive, generative monitoring. Integrating datasets across biometric identification, health, and behavioural clusters advance food security and animal welfare. Nevertheless, gaps in dataset diversity and standardisation hinder reproducibility, demanding an ethical shift toward data sustainability and computational efficiency.

title: Using a structured template to improve the “FAIRness” of datasets from agricultural research
abstract: Researchers increasingly aim to make field experiment datasets available to facilitate reuse. Such availability supports reproducibility, fulfills ethical obligations, and meets requirements from funding agencies seeking to maximize returns on investment. The FAIR principles (www.go-fair.org) specify that datasets should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. In agriculture, assessments indicate that while many datasets are findable and accessible, interoperability and reusability are often limited by the absence of widely adopted community standards for organizing data. In research on nutrient management for Florida agriculture, we developed a structured spreadsheet template to partially address gaps in interoperability and reusability. The template captures metadata, management practices (e.g., planting, irrigation, fertilization), measurements, soil descriptions, and daily weather. Each worksheet includes guidance on content, variable names, units of measurement, data formats, and example values. The structure parallels groupings in the data dictionary of the International Consortium for Agricultural Systems Applications (ICASA). Dictionary worksheets list all variable names, definitions, units, and equivalent ICASA terms to support interoperability. Software tools are provided to initialize and populate the template, including a quality assurance/quality control (QA/QC) tool that checks multiple aspects of dataset consistency, such as whether key dates are sequenced correctly, identifiers are consistent across worksheets, and all variables appearing in data sheets are defined in the dictionary. Example datasets from nitrogen management studies for three crops illustrate template use. The spreadsheet-based approach provides researchers with a simple and familiar platform for assembling datasets in a manner that enhances FAIR compliance, particularly with respect to interoperability and reusability.

title: Biomimetic and artificial intelligence-based variable-rate decoupling of water-use-environmental trade-offs under straw return in rice–wheat rotations
abstract: Combined strategies involving straw return and water management practices, such as furrow irrigation in direct-seeded rice systems, show varying performance in reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in rice–wheat rotations. However, achieving a reliable functional decoupling between the mechanized shallow-incorporated straw layer and the saturated subsurface water redistribution zone remains a key challenge, thereby limiting effective suppression of conditions that exacerbate methane (CH4) emissions. Additionally, decision support tools (DSTs) for optimizing freshwater demand, runoff recycling, and energy cost, while simultaneously reducing carbon dioxide (CO2) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions, remain underdeveloped. Further, robust frameworks capable of interpreting and translating data, simulations, and research findings into farmer-level decision-making to enhance the management of environmental trade-offs in rice–wheat rotations are still poorly defined. Therefore, this study proposes biomimetic tillage design and artificial intelligence (AI)-based DST by integrating a coupled Hydrus 2D/3D-MPC system with the generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) model to guide straw return and optimize water-energy use under a furrow-ridge system. Data collection, experiments, and model validation were conducted during the 2023 and 2024 rice seasons in Babaiqiao, Nanjing, China. Hydrus 2D/3D simulated wetting rates and soil moisture with an R2 of 0.80 and 0.89, respectively. For the biomimetic strategy, the optimized factors for straw-incorporated depth, plow pan thickness, and subsoiling depth were 6.50, 4.80, and 20.0 cm. Predictive control regulated conditions promoting GHG emissions while simultaneously optimizing water-energy use. The AI-based DST achieved performance score of 95.71 ± 0.68 %, translating simulations into clear guidance for farmers. Biomimetic stratification increased irrigation demand by 9.9 %, but integrating it with film mulching and runoff recycling significantly offset the increased freshwater requirement and reduced energy costs by 23.14 %. Overall, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of integrated multi-objective techniques for optimizing water-energy use, mitigating conditions that exacerbate GHG emissions, and reducing runoff-related environmental footprints in rice–wheat rotations.

title: Transfer learning-based feature and token fusion for detecting grapevine yellows from multispectral images
abstract: Grapevine yellows diseases-most critically Flavescence Dorée, alongside Bois Nois-pose a significant threat to viticulture. Their symptoms are frequently confounded with those of Leafroll, Esca, and leaf discoloration, particularly in Chardonnay varieties, creating a complex multi-class classification challenge. To address this, we propose a transfer learning-based feature and token fusion method to detect grapevine yellows diseases from heterogeneous multispectral grapevine leaf images. The softmax-based fusion leverages probability distributions across multiple image features, tokens, and their merged combinations in a ’FUSION’ model. Feature and token extraction are performed using CNN and BEiT models, which are pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset and fine-tuned on our dataset. A lightweight ’HEAD’ classifier ensures efficient computation. Our approach can also be applied to classic RGB images. Evaluated on four datasets, including three public RGB benchmarks, the method achieved 100% accuracy on a 6-class subset and 99.954% on all 38 classes of PlantVillage, together with 100% on an open-source Grapevine Disease Dataset and 99.238% on another AI challenge dataset. On our challenging multispectral grapevine yellows dataset (5 classes: healthy, grapevine yellows, leafroll, discoloration, and Esca), it attained 82.87% accuracy on the same-year test data and a robust 79.99% on unseen-year data. These results outperform state-of-the-art approaches, highlighting the method’s potential for detecting diseases when symptoms are subtle, easily confused, or vary across acquisition years, including when using RGB images.

title: Coupling modelling and validation of multi-modal intrinsic parameters of maize kernel based on discrete element method
abstract: This study aims to address the issue of breakage during sowing, threshing, and storage of maize kernels, which reduces the quality of mechanical operations. Using uniaxial compression tests, the peak load of maize kernels was determined under different moisture content, axial ratio, and pressure direction conditions. A constitutive model was developed to describe the moisture content, axial ratio, peak load, and displacement of maize kernels under abdominal pressure. Based on the principle of hexagonal closest packing, a particle model was constructed to precisely represent the outer contour and internal dense structure of maize kernels. The bonding parameters of the Bonding V2 model were calibrated through orthogonal experiments, and the theoretical load peak relative to the actual error was 1.7%. Explored how the required calibration parameters should change under the condition of 0.2-0.5 mm particle radius, the parameters corresponding to the particle with the current radius r0 are p, n, and s. Once the particle radius reaches r0/m, the corresponding parameters should be updated to m2p, m2n, and s. Through response surface analysis, a regression equation was developed that quantitatively relates moisture content, axial ratio, and bonding parameters to the maximum load and displacement of the bridge. The model’s relative error was 4.5%. By combining DEM-MBD simulation with bench testing, the model’s mechanical characterisation performance was verified. When the seeder’s forward speed is 8 km/h, the simulation results indicate that wear is most severe within the range from finger clamp closure to seed rotation of 40°. At this stage, the average resultant force on the kernels was 1.03N, and the bond fracture ratio was 2.49%. It can better characterize the sowing damage process. Research can provide a model to support reducing mechanical losses during maize sowing and threshing.

title: Interpretable ensemble learning facilitated digital mapping and driver assessment of soil available phosphorus
abstract: Soil available phosphorus is one of the key indicators of plant growth and soil fertility, and accurately and quantitatively mapping it is highly important. High-resolution soil mapping is necessary for soil management, but the applications of machine learning are still limited. The objective of the present study was to establish a stable and interpretable prediction model to map and explain the influence of environmental variables on the prediction of soil available phosphorus. Six machine learning models were tested at a spatial resolution of 30 m on the basis of data from 159 soil samples in North China, and ensemble models were established via the stacking method. Climate data, topography data, and remote sensing vegetation indices were used as inputs for the prediction of soil available phosphorus. The results showed that the ensemble models had higher accuracy than the machine learning models alone did, with a relative improvement of at least 33.3% in the coefficient of determination R2. The topographic variable dominated the prediction of soil available phosphorus, the climate variable affected the prediction in local areas, and the vegetation variable contributed to the prediction indirectly influenced by terrain and climate factors. Aspect, difference in vegetation indices and net primary productivity are the most important predictors.
