This study proposes PP-LLMs, an innovative framework that bridges visual perception and agronomic reasoning by integrating a lightweight detection model, YOLON, with a fine-tuned Large Language Model, Tomato-Qwen. Our core contributions are threefold. First, we constructed the TGMD (Tomato Growth Multimodal Dataset), a benchmark comprising 9,519 high-quality expert-annotated language pairs covering descriptions of tomato growth status and agricultural production knowledge.Second, we developed YOLON, which employs efficient DELK-Block and GSLK modules to achieve high-precision detection of tomato organs while maintaining a lightweight architecture suitable for real-time edge deployment. Third, by applying a two-stage fine-tuning process (LoRA and prompt learning) to Qwen-7B-Chat, we enabled Tomato-Qwen to perform complex agronomic reasoning based on real-time phenotypic and environmental data. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy significantly outperforms mainstream baselines. Tomato-Qwen achieved substantial improvements in QA tasks, with BLEU-4 and ROUGE-L scores increasing by 29.42% and 33.13% respectively.This research demonstrates the preliminary effectiveness of visual-language collaboration in agriculture and suggests a potentially scalable solution for autonomous greenhouse management. But the generated agronomic suggestions should be regarded as preliminary candidate outputs whose practical safety and reliability have not yet been validated by domain experts.

title: Retraction notice to “Shrimp larvae detection and counting in aquaculture using multiscale feature fusion networks” [Comput. Electron. Agric., 233 (2025) 109850]
Leaf- and canopy-level hyperspectral sensing of wheat-Fusarium head blight-Trichoderma gamsii interactions
abstract: Fusarium head blight (FHB) is a major mycotoxigenic disease of wheat, causing yield and quality losses and deoxynivalenol contamination. Rapid, non-destructive tools are needed to detect FHB, monitor wheat physiological responses, and evaluate sustainable management strategies, including biological control agents. Although vegetation spectroscopy is widely used for high-throughput phenotyping, most spectral studies focus on binary disease detection, while the capacity of hyperspectral data to capture concurrent host–pathogen–biocontrol responses across leaf and canopy scales remains underexplored. Here, we tested a full-range (400–2400 nm) hyperspectral phenotyping framework to track early interactions among winter wheat, FHB, and Trichoderma gamsii T6085. Two cultivars, Bingo and Rebelde, with higher and lower FHB susceptibility, respectively, were treated with a chemical fungicide (Chem) or T. gamsii T6085 (Bioc) under FHB pressure. Leaf- and canopy-level spectra were acquired at 2, 5, and 14 days post-inoculation, alongside gas exchange, water status, and chlorophyll measurements. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) tested whole-spectrum effects, partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) explored class separability, and partial least squares regression (PLSR) estimated physiological traits. PERMANOVA detected genotype × inoculation × treatment interactions from 5 days post-inoculation at leaf and canopy levels. PLS-DA revealed treatment- and cultivar-dependent spectral fingerprints, but overall low-to-fair validation performance indicates that these class-specific patterns should be interpreted as exploratory and not as evidence of operational treatment discrimination. PLSR provided high accuracy for chlorophyll content and osmotic potential, moderate accuracy for CO 2 -assimilation traits, and poor accuracy for transpiration and leaf water potential. While the workflow is scalable as an experimental and analytical framework, its operational deployment will require broader validation across sites, seasons, cultivars, disease-pressure conditions, and sensing platforms.

title: A Knowledge-Driven Cross-Modal fusion method for intelligent quality assessment of cabbage
abstract: The quality assessment of cabbage still relies predominantly on manual sensory evaluation, which is inherently subjective and inefficient. Moreover, a single nondestructive visual imaging modality often fails to provide robust grade classification for head cabbage under complex field conditions. To address these limitations, this study proposes a knowledge-driven two-stage cross-modal fusion framework for intelligent cabbage quality assessment, in which semantic priors and index priors are jointly leveraged to guide the inference process. The framework integrates RGB and multispectral imaging (MSI) data. In the first stage, semantic segmentation masks are employed to establish a mask-guided region-of-interest gating mechanism, thereby suppressing complex background interference and enabling region-level alignment of cross-modal features. In the second stage, multidimensional vegetation indices are extracted as prior knowledge and incorporated into the decision layer through a residual calibration mechanism, thereby compensating for the limited capacity of unimodal visual features to represent physiological semantics. Experimental results showed that the cross-modal fusion model achieved a classification accuracy of 96.00 % and an F1-score of 95.48 % in the cabbage quality grading task. While maintaining high accuracy, the model also exhibited low computational cost, with only 26.67 million parameters and an inference time of 5.36 ms. In addition, the model was evaluated on 10 held-out cultivars collected at the same site, during the same growing season, and under uniform agronomic management. This evaluation indicated preliminary transferability across cultivars under shared environmental conditions. By aligning structural features with spectral responses, this study provides a technical foundation for the nondestructive grading of head cabbage under open-field conditions.

title: Deep transfer learning for spectral prediction of kiwifruit quality across cultivars and instruments
abstract: The Vis/NIR detection of kiwifruit quality is limited by biological variations between cultivars and hardware response offsets among instruments. To address these challenges, a cross-cultivar and cross-instrument prediction method for soluble solids content (SSC) and firmness (FI) was developed by integrating a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) with deep transfer learning (DTL). The proposed approach mitigates spectral discrepancies arising from cultivar and instrument differences by freezing the convolutional layers and fine-tuning the fully connected layers. Spectral data of three representative kiwifruit cultivars were collected using two spectrometers. The 1D-CNN models developed using single-cultivar datasets achieved average residual predictive deviation (RPD) values of 3.2438 and 5.8899 for SSC and FI prediction, respectively. However, cross-cultivar validation experiments revealed that cultivar differences caused the 1D-CNN model to fail significantly. To address this, a DTL strategy that fine-tunes the fully connected layers while freezing the convolutional layers was proposed, outperforming conventional transfer learning methods. Using only 15% of the target-domain samples for fine-tuning, the DTL model achieved average RPD values of 1.9361 and 2.2015 for cross-cultivar prediction of SSC and FI, respectively. In simultaneous cross-instrument and cross-cultivar transfer scenarios, when QEPro was used as the master instrument and STS-NIR as the target, the DTL method achieved average RPD values of 2.6178 and 3.6796 for SSC and FI predictions across three cultivars. Similarly, with only 15% of the master instrument’s update samples, the DTL model provided reliable cross-instrument predictions (RPD > 1.5), effectively offsetting spectral shifts caused by instrument hardware variations. Furthermore, Gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) analysis revealed that the 810–1000 nm spectral region contributed most significantly to model adaptation, providing insights into the mechanism by which DTL enhances cross-domain performance through the reinforcement of informative spectral features. These results demonstrate the robustness of DTL for cross-cultivar and cross-instrument kiwifruit quality detection, providing support for the large-scale deployment of fruit quality monitoring systems.

title: Plant wearables in smart agriculture: advancements, technical challenges, opportunities, and a cyber-physical roadmap in volatile organic compound detection
abstract: The agricultural sector faces escalating challenges from climate-induced abiotic stressors, herbivory, and pathogens. Optimizing crop productivity requires advanced technologies for real-time monitoring. While volatile organic compounds (VOCs) serve as early-onset biomarkers for plant stress, conventional laboratory methods lack high-temporal resolution, and portable electronic noses suffer from limited selectivity. However, transitioning to in situ plant wearables is severely bottlenecked by critical research gaps: severe signal baseline drift caused by fluctuating ambient humidity crosstalk, stomatal shielding from non-porous substrates that disrupts natural leaf transpiration, and a computational void in deploying artificial intelligence for autonomous material stoichiometry optimization and real-time deconvolution of overlapping VOC profiles at the resource-constrained edge. To critically address these gaps, this review systematizes the transition toward Cyber-Physical Plant Systems (CPPS) via wearable VOC-sensing architectures. We evaluate the AI-material nexus, demonstrating how metaheuristic optimization and Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks like SHAP and LIME can autonomously optimize sensor materials and validate biogenic fingerprints. A central contribution of this work is a transdisciplinary and strategic four-phase technical roadmap integrating materials science, edge-computing, and Industry 5.0 principles. This framework outlines the engineering of transpirational-neutral architectures and low-power Edge-AI hardware to resolve multi-stressor profiles. By bridging the gap between plant metabolism and digital intelligence, this review provides a strategic pathway aligning with Agriculture 5.0 to build autonomous bio-information systems for enhanced agricultural resilience.

title: Spatiotemporal video encoder integrated with metadata fusion for action recognition and behavior analysis
abstract: Automated behavior monitoring and action recognition is challenging in dense, dynamic environments of broiler pens, combined with the challenges of handheld smartphone footage. This study developed and validated an integrated pipeline for spatiotemporal action recognition and behavioral analysis of individual broiler chickens using smartphone-captured video. Our end-to-end framework addresses key technical challenges by first stabilizing raw footage to correct motion artifacts, then employing YOLOv11-Pose for robust detection and pose estimation in crowded scenes, and ByteTrack for multi-object tracking. The core innovation is a novel metadata fusion strategy, where spatiotemporal features from an X3D video encoder were integrated with pose-derived contextual metadata (such as velocity and proximity to feeders and drinkers) using a multilayer perceptron. This intermediate fusion approach enabled the model to disambiguate visually similar but contextually distinct actions, such as drinking versus feeding. The system demonstrated strong performance on five key maintenance behaviors (resting, walking, standing, drinking, and eating), achieving an average F1-score of 0.864 and an overall test accuracy of 86.41 %. The system was particularly effective at detecting drinking and feeding behaviors, with individual F1-scores of 0.949 (94 % accuracy) and 0.928 (91.89 % accuracy) respectively. The system successfully processed 174 videos, producing valuable insights in the form of behavioral metrics, spatial heatmaps, and individual trajectories. This demonstrates that an integrated system, combining stabilization, advanced multi-task models, and contextual metadata fusion, can effectively use smartphone footage to create a scalable, objective tool for precision poultry farming and welfare research. The key advantages of the proposed framework include its ability to disambiguate visually similar birds and behavior actions through metadata fusion, its use of accessible cost-effective smartphone data, and its balance of accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: SPROUT: AI-based seedling emergence PRedictiOn and trait extraction using RGB time-series
abstract: Early crop establishment strongly influences plant performance and yield, making seedling emergence an important trait in crop phenotyping, breeding, and stress physiology studies. However, emergence monitoring is still commonly performed manually and typically records only the final emergence percentage, limiting the analysis to other dynamic observations. Automated image-based approaches are promising but remain challenging due to the small size of plant structures, heterogeneous soil backgrounds, and variability across imaging systems. Here, we present SPROUT (AI- based S eedling PR edicti O n and trait extraction U sing RGB T ime-series), a low-cost RGB imaging pipeline for automated prediction of crop emergence dynamics and trait extraction. The system integrates instance segmentation, object-detection–based data reduction, and temporal deep learning to estimate the emergence time of individual seedlings from RGB image sequences. The pipeline then automatically reconstructs emergence curves and extracts associated traits, including final emergence percentage, EC50, and emergence synchronicity. SPROUT was developed and evaluated using barley and wheat datasets acquired with different RGB cameras under controlled growth-chamber conditions. In the development and retraining settings, the best-performing TCN model achieved 90.0% per-well accuracy with a ± 2h tolerance, supporting accurate emergence curve reconstruction. In an independent inference-only dataset, the model still captured approximate emergence dynamics, although accuracy decreased to 59.3%, indicating that SPROUT is best used as a modular pipeline that can be retrained or fine-tuned for new crop, camera, or experimental domains. A cadmium-stress case study in two contrasting wheat genotypes showed that SPROUT-derived traits captured genotype-specific establishment strategies associated with growth and metabolic responses.

title: A robust rank aggregation based interpretable minimum predictor set for scalable soil organic carbon mapping
abstract: Digital soil monitoring depends on a difficult balance: models must be simple enough to support operational monitoring but still grounded in the environmental processes that control soil variation. However, current soil health assessments and mapping frameworks often depend on large covariate libraries that increase computational costs, introduce redundancy, and limit reproducibility across agroecological domains. This problem is particularly important for soil organic carbon (SOC), whose spatial distribution reflects interacting controls from climate, terrain, soil type, texture, vegetation, and land use. Here, we identify a minimum set of environmental predictors that is stable across selection algorithms and transferable to contrasting landscapes. Using 28,738 georeferenced topsoil samples from Ethiopia and 73 SCORPAN covariates, we benchmarked seven feature selection methods spanning filter, embedded, and wrapper families and integrated their rankings through robust rank aggregation. Models were evaluated on spatially disjoint highland, midland, and lowland test domains. The consensus set retained eleven predictors, dominated by soil texture, WRB reference soil group, and mean annual temperature, and explained 75 % of SOC variance. Relative to the full 73-covariate baseline, XGBoost trained on the reduced set lowered test RMSE by 25 %. SHAP analysis showed that the top three predictors accounted for 78 % of model attribution, indicating that the reduced set preserved the main pedogenic controls on SOC stabilization rather than simply removing redundant variables. The framework provides a parsimonious and interpretable basis for SOC prediction across heterogeneous landscapes, with direct relevance for scalable soil health monitoring, national carbon assessment, and precision land management decisions.

title: Robust autonomous navigation in unstructured orchards: Integrated LIO-SAM with NDT-based relocalization and Bayesian traversability mapping
abstract: Agricultural environments, particularly orchards, are characterized by their unstructured nature, irregular terrain, and lack of geometric features, posing significant challenges for robotic localization and navigation. This study presents an integrated navigation system tailored for such GPS-denied and feature-degraded environments. To constrain cumulative drift during long-term operations, we enhance the Tightly-coupled LiDAR Inertial Odometry via Smoothing and Mapping (LIO-SAM) framework by introducing an active relocalization module based on the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT). Unlike rigid pose resetting, this module integrates global registration constraints as dynamic factors into the factor graph, ensuring smooth and robust state estimation without trajectory discontinuities. Furthermore, to address complex terrain traversability, a continuous probabilistic map is constructed using Bayesian Generalized Kernel (BGK) inference, which explicitly models the uncertainty of terrain features. Based on the generated 2D traversability grid map, a dual-tree Rapidly-exploring Random Tree* (RRT*) planner is implemented for efficient path planning. Experimental results in real-world orchards show that the proposed system maintains bounded and continuous state estimates during extended traversals, identifies traversable areas amidst vegetation occlusion, and generates collision-free paths with practical computational efficiency. This work contributes a robust solution for enhancing the autonomy of agricultural robots in large-scale, complex scenarios.

title: Three-dimensional reconstruction and light interception quantification of maize/soybean system based on UAV cross-surround photography
abstract: [Background and objective] Maize/soybean intercropping performance is strongly influenced by three-dimensional (3D) canopy architecture, which regulates light interception and crop complementarity. This study aimed to reconstruct field maize/soybean canopies from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) RGB imagery and quantify how planting pattern and density affect canopy light distribution, yield, and land equivalent ratio (LER). [Method] Field experiments were conducted in northeast China using three row configurations (2:2, 2:4, and 4:4 maize/soybean strips) and three maize planting densities (6.4 × 104, 9.6 × 104, and 11.2 × 104 plants ha⁻1). Canopy structure was reconstructed using UAV RGB cross-surround imaging, structure-from-motion and multi-view stereo (SfM-MVS), and point-cloud processing. Reconstruction accuracy was evaluated using plant height, leaf length, and leaf width. The Helios light model was used to simulate canopy light interception and distribution. [Results] Plant height estimation achieved R2 values of 0.92 for maize and 0.72 for soybean, while leaf length and width estimates achieved R2 ≥ 0.88 and relative root mean square errors of 5–10 %. Helios simulations showed treatment-specific differences in canopy light distribution. At 102 days after emergence, maize light interception rate in medium-density 2:2 and 2:4 treatments exceeded 600 W m⁻2 during peak sunlight hours, whereas high-density treatments increased soybean shading. Medium-density treatments showed a favorable numerical balance between light capture and crop complementarity, with LER values of 1.06 ± 0.16 for 2:2M and 1.00 ± 0.04 for 4:4M; however, total LER was not significantly affected by planting density. [Conclusion] UAV RGB cross-surround imaging combined with SfM-MVS reconstruction and light-interception modeling provides an effective workflow for linking 3D canopy architecture, light acquisition, and yield formation. Medium-density configurations showed a favorable numerical balance between canopy light capture and interspecific complementarity.

title: PanicleScope-Net: A small-object-aware network for rice panicle segmentation in complex field scenes
abstract: Rice is a globally vital staple crop, precise identification of rice panicles is essential for yield estimation, pest and disease monitoring, and nutritional status assessment. However, complex field conditions characterized by occlusion, lighting variation, and background interference pose significant challenges to existing semantic segmentation models, particularly under limited computational resources. To address this issue, we propose a novel multi-objective architecture search method, ODR-IAS. The search space integrates a variety of convolutional and pooling modules, and is explored using a variable-length encoding strategy (VLES) and a dynamic decoding strategy (DDS) to enhance architectural flexibility and multi-scale feature representation. To balance segmentation accuracy and parameter complexity, we design a multi-objective fitness function (MOFF) that jointly considers segmentation accuracy and model size. Based on the optimal architecture, we propose a panicle segmentation model named PanicleScope-Net. Experimental results on a self-constructed rice panicle maturity dataset showed that the PanicleScope-Net achieves a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 90.27 %, with Precision, Recall, and F1-score values exceeding 95 %. Notably, models with comparable accuracy generally require substantially higher computational resources, whereas more compact models show clear accuracy degradation. These results demonstrate that the proposed method is effective for fine-grained small-object segmentation in complex field environments. Its low parameter count and FLOPs further indicate potential feasibility for future deployment in resource-constrained field applications.

title: Comprehensive low-damage mechanical weeding technology considering the spatial distribution of crop roots: A case study of maize farmland
abstract: Weed control is essential for improving fresh maize yield, and mechanical weeding is widely adopted in organic farming due to its environmental and economic advantages. Existing mechanical weeding equipment was not designed with the spatial distribution of crop root systems in mind, which can easily result in damage to the roots. To achieve comprehensive low-damage weeding, a mechanical weeding system integrating maize root spatial distribution characteristics with deep learning was developed. Firstly, morphological parameters of maize seedlings at the 3–5 leaf stage were measured, and an image dataset was constructed. Seedling detection was performed using the open-vocabulary model YOLOv8-world, achieving a precision of 0.958 and an average processing speed of 245.30 FPS on edge devices, which can meet the requirements for seedling recognition and detection in fresh maize field environments. Subsequently, based on the measured morphological parameters, a three-dimensional spatial protection zone was established. Four types of intra-row weeding knives with different angles were designed and tested in field experiments. Field experiments and variance analysis demonstrated that the intra-row weeding knife with a 20° angle was the most suitable for comprehensive low-damage weeding in fresh maize farmland. At an operational speed of 1.5 km/h, the average weed removing rate was 91.05%, with an average crop damage rate of 2.35%. The weeding system exhibited stable and reliable performance, making it suitable for comprehensive low-damage weeding operations in fresh maize farmland. This study provides a reference for the development of comprehensive low-damage weeding equipment.

title: An appearance-independent multi-object tracking framework for group-housed pigs
abstract: Accurate multi-object tracking of group-housed pigs is essential for health monitoring in precision livestock farming, yet remains challenging due to similar pig appearances, frequent occlusions, dense interactions, and nonlinear motion. This paper proposes STA-PigTrack (Spatiotemporal Association Enhanced Pig Tracking), an appearance-free tracking method based on enhanced spatiotemporal association. The method introduces the Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) to better handle nonlinear motion such as sudden accelerations and sharp turns, outperforming conventional Kalman-based models. To address identity loss from long-term occlusion and trajectory fragmentation, an AFLink module constructs a global cost matrix from spatiotemporal trajectory continuity, combined with the Hungarian algorithm to recover fragmented identities without relying on appearance embeddings. Evaluated on both a self-collected and a public dataset, STA-PigTrack achieved average HOTA, MOTA, and IDF1 scores of 83.82 %, 96.27 %, and 89.73 %, respectively, reducing identity switches by 70.2 % compared with the baseline SORT, while maintaining a real-time speed of 56 FPS. It outperformed DeepSORT, BotSORT, and OCSORT in identity consistency and robustness under heavy occlusion and high-density conditions. Using the obtained trajectories, group activity intensity and individual cumulative displacement were extracted as exploratory trajectory derived movement indicators, showing the feasibility of transforming tracking outputs into quantifiable behavioral features. STA-PigTrack provides a reliable real-time solution for individual tracking in complex farm environments and may provide a technical basis for future precision health monitoring and welfare related applications.

title: Long-term identity-consistent multi-pig tracking in group-housed pens
abstract: In intelligent and precision livestock farming, continuous individual-level tracking of group-housed pigs is essential for behavior monitoring and health management. However, in real-world group-housing environments, high appearance similarity among pigs, frequent occlusions, intensive interactions, and irregular motion patterns cause trajectory fragmentation and identity drift. Therefore, a long-term multi-pig tracking framework tailored for group-housed pig barn scenarios is developed in this study. Within a standard “detection–association–trajectory management” pipeline, data association is performed by jointly exploiting appearance features and motion information, with Re-identification-based appearance modeling. In addition, an identity memory bank and a trajectory relinking mechanism are introduced to enhance identity recovery following occlusions and reduce identity switches (IDSWs). The proposed framework was evaluated on real-world pig barn surveillance video data. Under same-scene conditions, the model demonstrated improved identity consistency and high tracking accuracy, achieving a multiple object tracking accuracy (MOTA) of 0.9010, an identity F1 Score (IDF1) of 0.6762, and an IDSW of 24, outperforming BoT-SORT (MOTA = 0.8673, IDF1 = 0.5675, IDSW = 40), ByteTrack (MOTA = 0.8585, IDF1 = 0.5735, IDSW = 30) and DeepSORT (MOTA = 0.8640, IDF1 = 0.5615, IDSW = 40). Moreover, under more challenging cross-scene conditions, partial generalization was still observed (MOTA = 0.7011, IDF1 = 0.0950, IDSW = 405), indicating transferability to scene variations, severe occlusions, and imaging noise. Overall, the proposed framework provides more reliable long-term individual-level trajectory acquisition for group-housed pigs, supporting behavior analysis and management decision-making in intelligent livestock farming. The method has been made publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/glimmerc33-ui/pig_track.git).

title: Bovine-LTID: A vision-based spatio-temporal identity system for multi-camera cattle tracking and long-term behavior monitoring
abstract: Multi-camera video monitoring of group-housed cattle is essential for health assessment in precision livestock farming, offering a scalable, non-invasive alternative to labor-intensive manual observations and restrictive wearable sensors. However, existing systems for cross-camera identity matching typically rely on computationally intensive appearance-based Re-identification (ReID). These approaches often struggle in dense barns due to frequent mutual occlusions, viewpoint variations, and the high visual similarity of cattle coat patterns. To address these limitations, we propose Bovine Long-Term Identity (Bovine-LTID), a resource-efficient, ReID-embedding-free spatio-temporal tracking framework for multi-camera behavior monitoring. Instead of relying on ambiguous appearance features, Bovine-LTID maintains identity consistency through spatial geometry and temporal logic. The system integrates a behavior-aware detector (YOLOv9s) with a cattle-optimized single-view tracker (CowTracker) to recover identities during prolonged occlusions. For cross-view synchronization, trajectories are projected into a unified ground-plane coordinate system via homography calibration and managed by a centralized Global ID Pool. Trained on NVIDIA H200 GPU, the detection module achieves a test-set mAP50 of 0.944, while the complete pipeline operates at approximately 13 FPS on consumer-grade hardware (NVIDIA RTX 4060 Laptop, 8 GB VRAM). The cross-camera fusion mechanism reduces global raw identity switches by 87.6% over single-camera baselines and achieves a 99.33% cross-view identity consistency. These findings present a practical methodology for scalable, automated herd welfare assessment spanning from high-performance training to edge deployment.

title: FedAD: Federated learning with generative data augmentation and adaptive parameter decomposition for rice pest and disease identification
abstract: Rice is a primary global food source, but its production is severely threatened by pests and diseases, leading to significant yield losses and economic instability. Traditional manual identification is labor-intensive and error-prone. Deep Learning (DL) offers automated and accurate diagnosis, but its centralized deployment raises data privacy concerns and incurs high communication costs. Federated Learning (FL) provides a privacy-preserving alternative, but it faces challenges such as statistical heterogeneity (Non-IID data) and stringent resource constraints in the Internet of Agricultural Things (IoAT). To address these issues, we propose a personalized framework called Adaptive Parameter Decomposition Federated Learning (FedAD). FedAD employs a strategy based on Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to decouple model weights into a shared full-rank component and a personalized low-rank component, and we introduce a dynamic rank allocation mechanism to adaptively adjust the personalized capacity for each client without requiring explicit SVD decomposition. In addition, we design a resource-efficient backbone model (SepResNet) to balance model performance with overall resource constraints in federated environments. To mitigate data scarcity and improve robustness, we construct a novel dataset (RP15) by employing a hybrid augmentation strategy that combines traditional transformations with generative AI synthesis. Experiments on both the RP15 dataset and the public PlantVillage dataset demonstrate the superior performance and generalization ability of FedAD. On the RP15 dataset, FedAD achieves 90.40% Accuracy, an 86.79% F1-Score, and 87.10% Recall, outperforming baseline methods by over 10% and doubling the convergence speed. On the PlantVillage dataset, FedAD achieves 99.45% Accuracy, a 99.04% F1-Score, and 99.12% Recall, significantly outperforming baseline models. Finally, we provide both experimental and theoretical validation of the framework’s convergence, which ensures training stability and offers guidance for hyperparameter selection. The source code and RP15 dataset are available at https://github.com/DongfuHou/FedAD.

title: DASNet: Dual-channel adaptive segmentation network for pigtail fork bone path generation
abstract: The unpredictable fracture or displacement of pigtail fork bones during slaughter, together with their low contrast against adjacent tissues, often results in blurred boundaries in X-ray images, posing significant challenges for robotic cutting. To support robotic cutting under such degraded imaging conditions, the X-ray Pig Bone Dataset (XPBD), is constructed, comprising 506 images of pigtail fork bones and 260 images of pig leg bones. Based on XPBD, a Dual-Channel Adaptive Segmentation Network (DASNet) is proposed for boundary-preserving segmentation under low-contrast and blurred conditions. DASNet integrates diffusion-based adaptive mask generation, learnable Gabor-based edge enhancement, and weighted multi-scale contextual feature fusion. The predicted segmentation mask is further converted into an ordered four-cut cutting path using a process-prior mask-to-path strategy and executed under compliant control with six-axis force and torque feedback. Experimental results on XPBD demonstrate that DASNet achieves superior segmentation performance compared with state-of-the-art methods, with an AP of 51.768% on the heterogeneous fuzzy subset. Cutting trials on an industrial workstation further validate the practical feasibility, demonstrating stable cutting performance with a coefficient of variation of 6.52%. Moreover, the proposed system has been successfully deployed on a pigtail fork bone cutting workstation at Jiangsu Huai’an Su Food Meat Co., Ltd., where dual robotic arms collaboratively mimic manual pigtail fork bone stripping from skinned pig carcasses.

title: TreePMNet: a deep matching network for registration of UAV and handheld LiDAR data in fine phenotyping of rubber plantations
abstract: Advanced phenotyping is essential for precise growth monitoring and reliable yield forecasting of economically significant rubber trees. Unmanned laser scanning (ULS) from an aerial perspective and handheld laser scanning (HLS) from the ground can efficiently capture 3D structural information of rubber plantations. Registering these two datasets can compensate for respective information gaps and achieve a more complete 3D representation. However, existing point cloud registration methodologies often suffer from low robustness or computational inefficiency when applied to forest scenes. This study proposes TreePMNet, a deep learning-based point cloud registration method. First, a Local Feature Aggregation (LFA) module is designed to generate salient keypoints and distinctive descriptors. Subsequently, a Progressive Transformation Estimation (PTE) module is used to achieve coarse-to-fine registration. The proposed method was evaluated using the public ULS-HLS-Rubber dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that TreePMNet facilitates both effective and efficient registration of ULS and HLS point clouds. The average RMSE, RRE, and RTE values reached 0.09 m, 0.17°, and 0.22 m, respectively. Furthermore, the average processing time for a 900 m 2 plot was only 0.98 s. The R 2 values for tree height, diameter at breast height (DBH), and crown diameter extracted from the registered point cloud data reached 0.989, 0.856, and 0.914, respectively. This study underscores the developmental potential of deep learning-based methods for ULS and HLS point cloud registration in complex forest environments. Our findings provide invaluable support for the accurate acquisition of 3D structural information and advanced phenotypic characterization in rubber plantations.

title: A novel test methodology for evaluating prescription-map-based ISOBUS variable rate sprayers in viticulture
abstract: The use of variable rate application (VRA) technology enables spatial- and demand-oriented application of plant protection products, thereby facilitating precise and efficient plant protection in viticulture. However, there is a lack of standardised test methods for validating dynamic application volume rates for VRA sprayers in specialty crops. This paper presents a test methodology to evaluate the performance of ISOBUS-compliant VRA sprayers using prescription maps by comparing prescribed and applied spray volumes under controlled test bench and real field conditions. Therefore, four different test scenarios were developed for both environments to enable a systematic assessment of dynamic variable rate behaviour, including fixed (Scenario 1) and variable application volume rates under varying driving speeds (Scenario 2) and prescribed volume rate levels (Scenario 3). Depending on the scenario, the applied spray volumes derived from manual reference measurements, ISOBUS task logs and external flow sensor data (Scenario 4) were compared with each other. Overall, the developed test scenarios offer a first structured approach to assess the performance of VRA sprayers under controlled test bench and field conditions. In the first three scenarios, RMSE values below 5 % indicate that manual reference measurements and ISOBUS task log data provide a consistent and reproducible basis for assessing VRA behaviour along entire vine rows. In contrast, flow measurements using external sensors positioned downstream of the PWM nozzles showed higher deviations (RMSE ≤ 7.7 %) under highly dynamic conditions, demonstrating limitations for accurate applied spray volume assessment in the present experimental configuration.

title: C2BPNet: a crop disease segmentation network based on context-content-boundary perception
abstract: Accurate segmentation of crop disease regions is crucial for disease monitoring, quantification, and precision spraying. However, disease spots in field images often show large-scale variation, blurred boundaries, and irregular shapes, and are also affected by complex backgrounds and illumination changes. This makes it difficult for existing methods to balance long-range context modeling and local boundary detail recovery. To address these challenges, we propose C2BPNet, a crop disease segmentation network based on Context-Content-Boundary Perception, aiming to jointly improve contextual representation, lesion-region perception, and boundary refinement. Specifically, we introduce a grayscale-guided geometric prior attention in the encoder, which combines grayscale structural texture cues with relative position encoding to construct geometric constraints. This guides the network to focus on structurally consistent regions and effectively suppresses background noise. In the decoding stage, we use a DSWA-based segmentation head to adapt feature sampling to irregular lesion shapes and recover finer boundary details. We conduct extensive experiments on the publicly available PlantSeg dataset and our self-built Downy-MildewSeg dataset. C2BPNet achieves competitive performance compared with various mainstream CNN and Transformer segmentation models. To promote real-world applications, we have developed a visual diagnostic system to segment field images and quantify disease-spot regions. Our code is available at https://github.com/JLab724/C2BPNet.git.

title: Design and experiment of a collision warning system for unmanned tractors based on real-time trajectory prediction
abstract: The collision warning model is a key technology in tractor safety assistance systems. With the large-scale application of autonomous tractors in field operations, ensuring safe responses to dynamic obstacles during multi-machine collaborative operations has become a critical challenge.This study designed a real-time trajectory prediction-based collision warning system for autonomous tractors to enable safe and efficient cooperation. It developed a self-organizing inter-machinery communication network via XBee Mesh technology, established a GST-MSDR trajectory prediction model, proposed a hierarchical collision warning strategy based on oriented bounding box theory, and implemented the real-time system on physical vehicles using the ROS2 framework.Tests showed the communication network had self-healing capability with zero packet loss within 100 m; the prediction model achieved an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.60 m and final displacement error (FDE) of 1.23 m in real scenarios, with collision warning accuracy reaching 91%. Field tests confirmed the system accurately captured steering behaviors (predicted trajectories matched actual ones) and identified risks at least 5 s in advance, ensuring operational safety in multi-machine collaboration.

title: Research on adaptive denoising methods and characteristic analysis of load signals in agricultural tractors
abstract: Tractor field-load signals are characterized by severe non-stationarity and multi-component coupling, causing conventional denoising methods to suffer from mode mixing, under-decomposition, or signal distortion. To overcome these limitations, this study presents an adaptive denoising method specifically designed for tractor load signals by integrating a modified particle swarm optimization algorithm (MPSO), variational mode decomposition (VMD), and an improved wavelet threshold denoising (IWTD) method. The MPSO-VMD front-end adaptively optimizes decomposition parameters via an asymmetric time-varying acceleration mechanism, reducing the mean number of convergence iterations by up to 37.9% and ensuring 90.0% optimization stability under severe 0 dB signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions. Effective intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) are selected using a threshold based on the mean permutation entropy for final IWTD reconstruction. Performance evaluation across SNR levels of 0, 5, 15, and 25 dB demonstrates that the proposed MPSO-VMD-IWTD approach significantly outperforms conventional baselines. Critically, under severe 0 dB SNR conditions, it reduces the root-mean-square error (RMSE) to 1.7614 N·m for unimodal signals and 15.0793 N·m for bimodal signals while preserving amplitude fidelity. Field-load characteristic analysis reveals a dominant low-frequency energy concentration below 10 Hz, governed by a superposition of stochastic variations (<2 Hz) and distinct periodic excitations. Specifically, based on soil mechanics literature, the periodic component concentrated within 2.0–2.5 Hz during moldboard plowing is inferred to arise from cyclic soil shear failure. In contrast, rotary tillage yields a dominant peak within 4.6–4.9 Hz that closely matches the blade shaft rotational frequency. Transition conditions mainly affect low-frequency random amplitudes but preserve the frequency and amplitude of periodic loads. These findings facilitate tractor load spectrum compilation and durability design, provide a valuable reference for soil-machine interaction signal processing, and offer a theoretical basis for energy management in hybrid electric tractors.

title: Numerical simulation of the effect of exhaust fan layout on indoor air quality in stacked-cage poultry buildings during winter
abstract: Indoor air quality in poultry buildings is crucial for chickens’ health and production performance, and is primarily determined by ventilation system. Generally, tunnel ventilation system is widely used in stacked-cage poultry buildings, which consist of side-wall inlets and end-wall exhaust fans. During winter, ventilation rates are significantly reduced to keep poultry buildings warm, leading to poor indoor air quality and non-uniform airflow distribution. Previous studies mainly focused on the inlet design, however, the effect of exhaust fan layout has received limited attention. This study employed computational fluid dynamics (CFD), validated with experimental data in a commercial stacked-cage poultry building, to simulate seven cases with different exhaust fan locations and heights. Airflow velocity, age of air, CO2 concentration, and NH3 concentration were systematically analyzed to evaluate the indoor air quality. The performance of the optimized exhaust fan layout under colder climatic conditions, as well as its sensitivity, uncertainty, and energy consumption characteristics are further discussed. Results show that: (1) installing exhaust fans on both the front and end walls significantly enhances both airflow distribution uniformity and ventilation efficiency, with maximum improvements of 21.1 % and 26.4 %, respectively; (2) this layout also yields the lowest CO2 (NH3) concentrations and the most uniform distribution of CO2 (NH3), with a concentration decrease of 10.3 % (14.8 %) and a uniformity increase 75.4 % (70.7 %); (3) exhaust fan height has little effect on airflow distribution and indoor air quality, with environmental parameter differences remaining within ± 5 %, due to the rapid attenuation of airflow near exhaust fans. This study can provide practical guidance for optimizing ventilation system design and operation in stacked-cage poultry buildings during winter.

title: Application research on the mechanism of antlion vibration for reducing resistance and energy consumption in subsoiler
abstract: Subsoiling operations can effectively break the plow pan of the soil, thereby improving soil structure and promoting root growth and water infiltration. However, subsoiling operation faces challenges such as high resistance and high energy consumption, especially at the front of the subsoiler is prone to form large soil nuclei, resulting in a sharp increase in resistance. In this study, a high-frequency controllable vibration mechanism inspired by antlion biology for subsoiling resistance reduction and energy consumption reduction, is proposed, aiming to reduce resistance and saving energy during subsoiling operations by adjusting the vibration frequency. Through the derivation of the theoretical model, we systematically analysed the effects of various parameters in the subsoiling process on the reduction of resistance and energy consumption of controlled vibratory subsoiling, and further field experiments not only verified the validity of the theoretical model, but also visually demonstrated the significant resistance reduction effect of high-frequency vibration in actual subsoiling operation. The results show that the theoretical model of vibratory subsoiling operation can better reflect the actual subsoiling resistance, and illustrate the resistance reduction and energy consumption reduction effect of high-frequency controlled vibration subsoiling operation. The vibration subsoiling was able to reduce resistance by more than 20% compared with a subsoiler without a vibration source, with only a slight increase in energy. The results of the study provide a new idea for the resistance reduction design of subsoiler, and play a certain guiding significance for the vibration resistance reduction design of other soil-engaging components.

title: Intelligent integration in agricultural insect management equipment: applications, challenges, and future directions
abstract: As the most biodiverse group on Earth, agricultural insects have a significant impact on food security and daily life. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the applications, innovations, and future development directions of insect management devices from both hardware and software perspectives. Regarding intelligent software integration, the paper reviews key technologies in entomological research, focusing on agricultural insect detection, classification, monitoring, and phenotypic analysis. These technologies utilize image processing and computer vision techniques to achieve pest control in agricultural environments. This paper reviews the latest advancements in insect management methodologies over the past five years, with particular emphasis on their applications in insect population management and visualization. Regarding intelligent hardware integration, the paper introduces data collection devices specifically designed for insects, as well as novel field-based pest monitoring and management equipment, and elaborates on the working mechanisms and applicable scenarios of representative new equipment. Furthermore, this review categorizes and discusses the advantages and challenges of various types of insect management equipment. Finally, through a comprehensive literature analysis, this paper identifies future research directions, such as applying cutting-edge multimodal fusion technologies and large language model to pest management tasks. The findings of this review will serve as a reference for researchers and agricultural technicians developing advanced pest management models and equipment.

title: Satellite-anchored UAV sensing system for high-resolution soil moisture mapping
abstract: Soil moisture is a key indicator of crop water stress, yet developing high-resolution surface soil moisture maps for field-scale irrigation management remains challenging. Satellite-based optical models such as the Optical TRApezoid Model (OPTRAM) enable scalable estimation, but their spatial resolution is often too coarse for farm-level irrigation decisions. OPTRAM also relies on shortwave infrared (SWIR) reflectance, which is typically unavailable from UAV-mounted multispectral cameras, thereby limiting its direct use for UAV-based soil moisture estimation. This work addresses these spatial and spectral limitations through a satellite-anchored UAV sensing and processing framework for high-resolution surface soil moisture mapping. In the proposed framework, we first align and aggregate UAV multispectral imagery to the Sentinel-2 10 m grid for band-specific calibration. Then, we train a Random Forest model to learn the mapping from calibrated UAV Visible and Near-Infrared (VIS-NIR) bands to Sentinel-2 SWIR2 reflectance, generating a virtual SWIR2 band that enables OPTRAM-based surface soil moisture retrieval at native UAV resolution. The framework was evaluated over a 100-acre irrigated wheat field using 11 UAV campaigns conducted from December 2023 to April 2024 with a DJI Matrice 300 RTK and MicaSense RedEdge-MX Dual payload. Radiometric consistency with Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface reflectance was high (R>0.94, MAE<0.0031, ubRMSE<0.007). Field-aggregated UAV surface soil moisture estimates were consistent with the NASA SMAP/Sentinel-derived 1 km product across the campaign period (R>0.9, MAE<0.0303 m3m−3, ubRMSE<0.04 m3m−3). Point-scale validation against four calibrated near-surface in-situ sensors installed at 5 cm depth yielded low mean point-scale errors (MAE=0.0525m3m−3,ubRMSE=0.0353m3m−3) and moderate mean sensor-wise correlation (R=0.6908), reflecting the expected representativeness gap between UAV-derived surface retrievals and localized sub-surface sensor measurements. To support reproducibility and facilitate future research in UAV-based surface soil moisture mapping for field-scale irrigation management, we release the open-source processing pipeline.

title: DEM-MBD coupled simulation for quantifying seedbed compaction and wheat emergence force during post-sowing wheat compaction
abstract: Post-sowing compaction (PSC) is a key operation for regulating wheat seedbed conditions and emergence quality, but the effects of operating parameters on post-compaction seedbed structure, soil-seed contact (SSC), and emergence force (EF) remain insufficiently quantified. In this study, a compaction roller-soil DEM-MBD coupled model and a mechanically equivalent wheat emergence DEM model were established for a self-propelled intelligent wheat compactor (SIWC). The effects of forward speed and ballast load on soil penetration resistance (SPR) and post-compaction sowing depth (PCSD) were analysed, while SSC and EF were further evaluated under selected post-compaction seedbed states, with the number of contacts (NC) and normal overlap (NO) used to quantify SSC and field post-emergence establishment indicators used as supporting evidence. The model reproduced PCSD with relative errors of 3.54%-4.27%. Increasing ballast load increased post-compaction SPR and reduced PCSD, whereas increasing forward speed weakened soil compaction and increased PCSD. Compared with the non-compacted control (CK), PSC increased the average EF during the mechanically equivalent wheat emergence process from 3.63 N to 6.33–8.09 N, mean NC from 30.44 to 36.72–42.48, and mean NO from 0.08 mm to 0.13–0.14 mm. Field results showed that PSC increased tiller number and root number, although this promoting effect weakened under higher compaction levels. These results clarify how PSC operating parameters regulate seedbed compaction, sowing depth, SSC, and EF, thereby providing a theoretical basis for suitable wheat seedbed preparation and the selection of appropriate PSC operating parameters.

title: Quantification of group and individual behavioural responses to a nutritional challenge in dairy goats
abstract: Monitoring individual animal behaviour using sensor technology provides valuable insights into adaptation to environmental challenges. This study investigates the effects of a controlled nutritional challenge on the behavioural patterns of dairy goats using accelerometer-derived behavioural data. Fourteen goats were equipped with collar-mounted accelerometers for 19 days, including two days of nutritional challenge in the middle. The challenge consisted of a 7-day control period with standard total mixed ration (TMR), 2 days of straw feeding only, and a 10-day recovery period on the TMR. The ACT4Behav pipeline was used to classify behaviour from accelerometer data, and multiple features were extracted to characterize activity profiles. Post-challenge behaviours were compared to pre-challenge ones, considered as baseline. At the group level, mixed linear model analysis showed that rumination time decreased during the nutritional challenge, while time spent with the head in the feeder increased, particularly during the day. Lying time remained unchanged during the day but increased at night. At the individual level, high variability in behavioural responses was observed. Two novel indices, the Challenge Effect Index (CEI) and the Recovery Index (RI), were introduced to characterise the diversity of behavioural responses and recovery strategies among goats. While some goats fully recovered their baseline behavioural patterns, others exhibited higher levels of certain behaviours after the challenge. These results demonstrate that group-level analyses are not sufficient to assess the impact of environmental challenges, as individuals may have different response strategies.

title: Modelling the shapes of agricultural materials in DEM: methods, advances, and challenges
abstract: The selection of particle shape representation is fundamental to reliable and efficient Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations of agricultural processes, as the shape model influences microscale contact mechanics, macroscale bulk behaviour, and overall computational cost. Agricultural materials exhibit substantial morphological diversity, ranging from near-spherical grains to elongated stems, thin flexible leaves, and complex mixture and composite systems, which poses significant challenges for shape modelling in DEM. This paper presents a systematic review of state-of-the-art DEM shape modelling approaches for agricultural materials. DEM shape modelling approaches are categorised into single-element and multi-element models, and commonly used representations are critically compared. Shape measurement and characterisation methods are reviewed, covering techniques applicable to different particle size scales and the conversion of measured shapes into DEM particle models. Agricultural materials are classified into four morphological types, namely granular-type, rod-type, shell-type, and mixture and composite systems, and shape modelling strategies for each material type are examined. Based on a critical analysis of the trade-off between geometric fidelity and computational efficiency, a hierarchical decision framework is proposed to guide the selection of appropriate shape models according to material characteristics, process requirements, and available computational resources. Finally, key challenges and future research directions are identified, including rapid and low-cost shape measurement techniques, the development of unified contact modelling frameworks for mixed shape representations, and systematic hybrid shape modelling strategies for mixture and composite agricultural systems. This review provides a comprehensive methodological reference for researchers and practitioners engaged in DEM modelling of agricultural materials.

title: VMMFNet: a lightweight dual-branch multispectral fusion network for multi-stage detection of pine wilt disease
abstract: Pine wilt disease (PWD), caused by the pine wood nematode, seriously threatens pine ecosystems and forest management. Accurate early detection is essential for controlling its spread, but existing UAV-based methods mainly rely on visible-light images and often fail to capture weak physiological stress before obvious crown discoloration appears. To address this limitation, controlled inoculation experiments were conducted from April to July to analyze spectral dynamics. RedEdge, near-infrared (NIR), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), and Normalized Difference Red Edge Index (NDRE) were identified as sensitive features. Comparative experiments showed that the six-channel configuration of RGB, RedEdge, NIR, and NDVI was more suitable under the tested conditions. Based on this configuration, we propose VMMFNet, a lightweight dual-branch visible–multispectral fusion network for UAV-based multi-stage PWD detection. VMMFNet uses a dual-branch backbone to extract RGB structural cues and multispectral physiological cues separately. Lightweight Attention Block (LWABlock) and Multi-Scale Attention Aggregation (MSAA) enhance weak disease-related features with low computational cost. An MSAA-enhanced High–Low Attention Fusion (HLAF) module improves high–low feature interaction in the neck, and P2–P5 detection heads are constructed for stage-aware prediction. Three independent runs show that VMMFNet achieves AP-Early@0.5 of 85.6 ± 0.86%, mAP@0.5 of 88.40 ± 0.53%, and F1-score of 88.05 ± 0.74%, with 4.38 M parameters and 83.6 FPS. Compared with the best competing baseline, AP-Early@0.5 and mAP@0.5 are improved by 9.2 and 10.1 percentage points. Overall, VMMFNet is suitable for large-scale UAV image analysis and provides a potential basis for future lightweight deployment in forest disease monitoring.

title: KWATCHNet: Fusion of CNNs and BoVW-based features for potato leaf disease classification
abstract: Potatoes are one of the most widely produced crops worldwide. However, potato yield is significantly affected by fungal diseases, among which early blight and late blight are two of the most widespread and economically damaging. Timely identification of these diseases is crucial to minimising crop damage and supporting sustainable farming practices. In this study, we propose KWATCHNet, a hybrid classification model that integrates deep and handcrafted visual features for robust identification of potato leaf disease. A lightweight architecture, InceptionViT, is introduced for deep feature extraction, which combines Inception-Residual blocks enhanced with Squeeze-and-Excitation modules and a Transformer layer. Deep and handcrafted features are fused and refined using Principal Component Analysis (PCA), then classified using a Support Vector Machine (SVM). In the experimental work, four datasets were used, including three publicly available datasets collected under controlled conditions and one newly created real-world dataset (D4) collected by the authors in Punjab, India, under natural lighting conditions, with varied backgrounds and real farm environments. KWATCHNet achieved 99.81% accuracy on the PlantVillage dataset (USA), 99.79% on the Plant Leaf dataset (Pakistan) and 99.42% on the Kaggle dataset (Ethiopia). On the real-world D4 dataset, the model achieved an accuracy of 93.34%, demonstrating strong generalisation capability across both controlled and uncontrolled conditions. Grad-CAM++ visualisations validate that the model focuses on disease-affected regions, confirming the interpretability of the proposed fusion strategy. KWATCHNet offers a lightweight, interpretable model suitable for scalable, practical deployment in real-world conditions.

title: Volumetric cooling efficiency for the wet curtain in agricultural buildings: modelling and application
abstract: Wet curtains are the core cooling equipment in agricultural buildings such as greenhouses and livestock facilities, where cooling efficiency serves as the key evaluation index. Existing studies mostly fit the empirical correlations of cooling efficiency via field tests, which fail to elucidate the heat-mass transfer mechanisms and ignore material cost, thus limiting their guidance for practical design and operation. To address this, a new index, volumetric cooling efficiency, was proposed in this study, which integrates both cooling performance and material cost of wet curtains. A mechanism-based mathematical model for this index was established by coupling theoretical derivation with experimental measurement, and validated through wind tunnel experiments on 7060-type wet curtains with a relative error below 10 %. A commercial layer breeder house was selected as an application study to optimize the air velocity across wet curtains based on the volumetric cooling efficiency model, and the chicken heat stress was further assessed. Results show volumetric cooling efficiency rises then falls with increasing air velocity, achieving maximum values of 0.0940, 0.1342, and 0.1727 m−3 for wet curtains with thicknesses of 0.10, 0.15 and 0.20 m, respectively. Notably, operating the 0.20 m thick wet curtain at its optimal air velocity for maximum volumetric cooling efficiency may lead to the heat stress in chickens. The established model of volumetric cooling efficiency in this study can provide a quantitative and practical basis for the optimal design and efficient operation of wet curtains, helping to maintain suitable thermal environment and improve production performance in agricultural buildings.

title: AgrospAI: A data space for sovereign data sharing and on-demand AI services in agriculture
abstract: Digital transformation in agriculture is often hindered by stakeholders’ reluctance to share sensitive operational data. While regulatory pressures for environmental sustainability increase, farmers lack tools to demonstrate compliance without relinquishing control over their data. This paper presents AgrospAI, an agricultural data space demonstrator that is designed to ensure data sovereignty by design. Unlike traditional platforms that require data transfer, AgrospAI utilizes a “Compute-to-Data” (C2D) paradigm. We first demonstrate this via a high-value use case in the Spanish pig farming sector: a sovereign workflow for environmental certification. This system enables farmers to generate verifiable compliance reports while keeping raw sensor data localized and private. Additionally, we showcase a second use case: an on-demand semantic mapping that lowers entry barriers for heterogeneous data sources, allowing data to be shared as-is and mapped and integrated when needed. Our results indicate that AgrospAI provides an environment designed to support trust in which data providers remain sovereign, even when integrating data from diverse sources, and consumers receive actionable insights (e.g., sustainability scores) without ever accessing the providers’ underlying raw datasets. This helps mitigate the risks of data leakage and unauthorized reuse, may help address some of the barriers that hinder data sharing, and enables value generation from data that would otherwise remain unused.

title: LefNet: Lightweight Explainable Fast-trained Network for wheat growth prediction and mechanism resolving
abstract: Purpose: Investigating mechanisms of crop growth through neural networks presents significant challenges in AI-for-agriculture, since end-to-end deep learning models usually considered as “black-box” and lack interpretability. Method: To solve this issue, we propose LefNet, a Lightweight, Explainable and Fast-trained neural Network for crop growth prediction and mechanism resolving. The core improvement of LefNet is to replace neural connections between layers with Taylor polynomials, whose coefficients are learned during the training of crop growth prediction. Leveraging the parallel-friendly nature of polynomials, LefNet improves computational efficiency by avoiding computationally expensive recursive operations, while also recovering symbolic relationships among variables through finite polynomial expressions. This design both reduces model complexity and generates interpretable symbolic formulas that contains insights of the underlying growth mechanisms. Such polynomials are not the actual mechanism, but they consist unique understandings for further mechanism verification. Results: For the experiment, considering diverse fertilization strategies and sowing dates, we collected a simulated time-series data set reflecting multiyear wheat growth in northeast China to verify the performance of LefNet in both time series forecasting and mechanistic resolving. The performance of LefNet in crop growth forecasting surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, decreasing 7.5% of mean square error (MSE) with 26.8% improvement of training efficiency, and its recovery of relationships is also validated by the existing literature. Conclusion: These results indicated that our interpretable model achieves accurate crop growth prediction while providing interpretable symbolic expressions that may offer insights into the underlying growth mechanisms, suggesting a promising direction for developing lightweight and explainable crop growth prediction models. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lsl3/LefNet.

title: TSA-GAIN method for greenhouse environment data imputation based on encoder and dynamic hint matrix
abstract: Missing data in greenhouse environmental monitoring may substantially compromise the accuracy of predictive models and the effectiveness of control strategies. To address long-gap missing data and the fragmentation of cross-sensor coupling features in greenhouse environmental datasets, this study improves the Generative Adversarial Imputation Network (GAIN) and proposes a Two-Stage Adaptive Generative Adversarial Imputation Network (TSA-GAIN). The main innovations are as follows: an adaptive hint-rate function is designed to optimize the missing-value localization guidance mechanism. By leveraging the dynamic balance between generator and discriminator adversarial losses, the hint rate is updated adaptively, replacing the fixed hint-rate setting in conventional GAIN and thereby constructing a dynamic hint matrix to improve the training process. In addition, the model architecture is enhanced by introducing an encoder module at the front end of the generator. By embedding the distributional characteristics of the original data and the spatiotemporal correlations among variables into the latent noise vector, the model can generate samples more realistically and more stably, effectively addressing the slow convergence and unstable imputation caused by GAIN’s reliance on random noise. Experimental results show that TSA-GAIN significantly outperforms GAIN on three imputation metrics, with MAE reduced by 51.8%, RMSE reduced by 48.7%, and the correlation coefficient increased by 61.7%. Moreover, under high missing rates, the proposed method outperforms traditional approaches such as RF, KNN, and MICE, which can better adapt to the nonlinear relationship in greenhouse climate characteristics.

title: An integrated framework for winter wheat biomass remote sensing estimation through Phenological-Spectral fusion
abstract: Accurate aboveground biomass estimation of winter wheat is essential for precision agriculture, yet integrating multi-source phenological and spectral information while accounting for inter-annual variability remains challenging. This study presents an integrated remote sensing framework combining Boruta-SHAP-based feature selection, phenological metric integration, and hierarchical dual-layer attention mechanisms to estimate wheat biomass across multiple growing seasons. The framework comprises three complementary components: (1) Boruta-SHAP algorithm for systematic spectral feature selection; (2) integration of physiologically meaningful phenological metrics (Growing Degree Days, Growth Days, and Zadoks Scale) with selected spectral features; (3) dual-layer attention mechanism that dynamically weights feature importance, capturing complex temporal-spectral interactions. Validation using chronological partitioning (2012–2020 training, 2021–2022 testing) on a decade-spanning dataset (1,336 samples) demonstrates the framework’s capability to predict biomass in independent future years. Boruta-SHAP identified 27 physiologically relevant spectral features across visible, red-edge, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared regions. With ground-measured phenology, the model achieved R2 = 0.847 and RMSE = 1,575 kg/ha, representing a 16.7 % improvement in R2 and a 25.2 % RMSE reduction compared to spectral-only approaches, with a 49.3 % reduction in training iterations; when phenological indicators were instead estimated from spectral data to form a fully remote configuration, accuracy remained high (R2 = 0.822). SHAP analysis revealed that phenological indicators contributed 31.5 % to model performance, with spectral features providing complementary contributions. This integrated, explainable framework enables multi-year biomass forecasting at the site level, supporting precision agriculture decision-making.

title: Technology Acceptance Level (TAL): A human-centred metric for evaluating trustworthy artificial intelligence in agriculture
abstract: Artificial intelligence ( AI ) systems are increasingly proposed for agricultural decision support, precision farming and precision livestock farming ( PLF ), yet large-scale and durable adoption by practitioners remains the exception rather than the rule. Established maturity scales such as the Technology Readiness Level ( TRL ) capture the engineering progression of a technology from basic principles to operational deployment, but they are agnostic to whether end users actually rely on the resulting system in their daily work. This paper introduces the Technology Acceptance Level ( TAL ) as a complementary, human-centred metric for evaluating the usability, trustworthiness and operational uptake of AI in agriculture. TAL is defined as a nine-level ordinal scale, anchored in the Technology Acceptance Model and the European Union ethics guidelines for Trustworthy AI , that captures the trajectory from initial exposure of a system to a practitioner up to its stable, autonomous integration into routine decision-making. Each level is operationalised by a small set of measurable criteria spanning perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, transparency, reliability under changing conditions, and alignment with agricultural workflows. We provide a mathematically grounded aggregation rule based on a non-compensatory, minimum-of-dimensions principle that prevents a single weak dimension from being masked by strong scores elsewhere, and we derive a confidence interval for TAL estimates from practitioner survey data. The framework is illustrated through three representative use cases — variable-rate nitrogen management in arable cropping, vision-based fruit detection for selective harvesting, and computer-vision-based lameness detection in dairy cattle — each a distinct agricultural AI system, chosen to demonstrate how systems of comparable engineering maturity can occupy very different acceptance levels and, in particular, how the dimension that limits acceptance differs systematically across deployment contexts. By explicitly addressing the human-in-the-loop, TAL is proposed as a diagnostic instrument — subject to empirical validation — for identifying adoption barriers, prioritising iterative system improvement, and steering the transition from technically functional prototypes to practically accepted, trustworthy AI in the agri-food sector. The framework is developed and illustrated within a high-income, European-influenced agricultural context, and its scores in this article are illustrative rather than empirically measured. Two limitations bound these claims and should be read alongside them: the framework has not yet been validated against field data, and it is scoped to decision-support and monitoring AI , so that systems relying on physical actuation — and settings beyond the Western commercial context in which it was developed — require further extension.

title: DAU-Net: A density-adaptive unified attention network for long-tail fish counting in aquaculture
abstract: Accurate fish counting is crucial for fisheries resource assessment and intelligent aquaculture management. However, the long-tail problem caused by uneven density distribution—namely, undercounting in high-density areas owing to occlusion and overcounting in low-density areas owing to background interference affects counting accuracy. To address this issue, we propose a density-adaptive unified attention framework. This framework first enhances the individual discrimination ability for high-density areas via hierarchical cross-window fusion attention, which performs fine-grained modeling within the window and cross-window information fusion, resolving the undercounting bias in high-density areas. It then suppresses background noise in low-density areas by generating spatial saliency priors and applying attention bias in the spatial importance prior attention module, resolving the overcounting bias in low-density areas. Comparative experimental results on the underwater grass carp counting dataset demonstrated that our method reduces the mean absolute error by 7.2% and root mean square error by 7.0% compared with a suboptimal method. Our method also performs well on the carp count dataset and dense grass carp counting dataset. It provides strong support for accurate intelligent fish counting and is of significance for promoting sustainable fisheries.

title: LiDAR in precision agriculture for orchards and perennial tree crops: bibliometric analysis, sensor technologies, and algorithmic workflows
abstract: Orchards and perennial tree crops are economically and nutritionally vital components of global agriculture, yet their heterogeneous canopy architectures, long production cycles, and complex management requirements pose persistent challenges for reliable, scalable, and repeatable monitoring in support of precision management. Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) provides three-dimensional information on canopy architecture, tree structure, terrain, and orchard infrastructure, making it a key technology for perennial crop sensing. This review synthesizes LiDAR research in orchards and perennial tree crops from three perspectives: bibliometric development, sensor and platform evolution, and data-processing workflows. A curated corpus of 288 publications covering 24 crop types was analyzed to characterize temporal trends, crop representation, platform adoption, retrieved parameters, and publication patterns. The results show rapid growth after 2015, driven by UAV-based mapping, mobile laser scanning, compact multi-beam sensors, and increasing demand for structure-aware crop monitoring, while many tropical and subtropical perennial crops remain underrepresented. LiDAR systems are reviewed according to dimensionality, ranging principle, backscatter sampling, structural configuration, deployment platform, measurement attributes, field-condition robustness, and task-specific suitability. Processing workflows are then examined, including preprocessing, registration and SLAM, noise filtering, ground classification, segmentation, machine learning, deep learning, data fusion, and open-source software ecosystems. As the technical component of a two-part review series, this review emphasizes bibliometric trends, sensor technologies, and algorithmic workflows, complementing a companion review focused on LiDAR applications, implementation challenges, and management-oriented opportunities in orchard systems. Particular attention is given to orchard-specific bottlenecks, including canopy occlusion and beam attenuation, non-random missing data, repetitive-row registration drift, wind-induced canopy motion, radiometric inconsistency, limited model transferability, and computational constraints for real-time deployment. By integrating bibliometric evidence, sensor-system analysis, and algorithmic evaluation, this review identifies key priorities for future LiDAR in orchard research: standardized metadata and quality-control reporting, task-specific validation, occlusion-aware modeling, radiometric normalization, multi-platform fusion, transferable learning, and uncertainty-aware digital orchard modeling. Overall, LiDAR is positioned as a methodological foundation for reproducible phenotyping, precision orchard management, robotic perception, and data-driven perennial crop production.

title: Improving multi-view video fusion and model generalization in pig behavior monitoring with teacher–student semi-supervised learning
abstract: Single-view monitoring systems have been widely adopted in pig behavior detection due to their simplicity, low computational cost, and ease of deployment. However, these systems are limited by challenges such as occlusion, viewpoint bias, and incomplete scene coverage, which hinder continuous observation of individual pigs and reduce the reliability of behavioral measurements in dynamic housing environments. In light of these limitations, researchers have increasingly turned to multi-view systems, which leverage complementary perspectives to better capture pig behavior and alleviate information loss caused by crowding and social interactions, but existing multi-view approaches often struggle with multi-view video annotation and face challenges in maintaining consistent identification of pigs across viewpoints due to appearance variations. To address these issues, we propose a multi-view video fusion and model generalization method integrated with a Teacher–Student semi-supervised learning framework, which utilizes pseudo-label transfer to reduce the reliance on large-scale manual annotation and introduces strategies based on overlap area and ratio to reduce identity mismatching in bounding box mapping and enhance cross-view behavioral consistency. The framework further enables stable cross-view identity association, supporting longitudinal analysis of individual animals under complex occlusion conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that our method not only improves detection accuracy but also achieves superior generalization performance with limited labeled data, while simultaneously providing reliable multi-object tracking capability to support longitudinal behavioral monitoring and health-related analysis.

title: Development of a new spherical water sensor for detecting droplets deposition using variable resistor
abstract: Monitoring pesticide deposition is important for improving spray efficiency and reducing environmental and health risks.
